Guimaraes, who joined the Magpies in 2022 from Lyon for £40m, has made 195 appearances for Newcastle, scoring 31 goals.

Earlier on Monday, Guimaraes was on his way to meet up with Newcastle United at their pre-season camp in Spain.

He had left Brazil on Sunday, when it was widely reported he was expected to be arriving in La Manga.

However, Guimaraes is arriving at the Spain training camp in agreement with the club and is now set to join the group.

Last week, he called now departed head coach Eddie Howe the "king of this club" following his exit from St James' Park.

Howe's resignation came amid Arsenal's interest in Guimaraes, who has praised his former boss.

In an Instagram post, Guimaraes wrote the words over a picture of Howe: "King of this club!! Thanks for everything you've done for us.

"I loved enjoying our time together. Thanks for making me a better player and person! No words I can say will really say how much I enjoyed being our player. Wish you all the very best in your future, gaffer."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Sky Sports FC, Jay Boothroyd says Declan Rice and Bruno Guimaraes together as a midfield pair for Arsenal would be the best partnership in the Premier League.

'Interesting chess game begins' between Arsenal and Newcastle

Football expert Julian Laurens on Sky Sports News:

"You knew Newcastle would go into these negotiations trying to get as much money as possible from Arsenal.

"But we've seen from Arsenal this summer they won't pay over the odds, what they believe is the value of a player - Bruno Guimaraes, Morgan Rogers, Diomande and others.

"It's an interesting chess game starting between Newcastle and Arsenal. I believe between the player and Arsenal there were never going to be any problems, so it's between the clubs.

"That first bid was always going to happen about now, it was always going to be rejected. Now, the two clubs can discuss it a bit more.

"I think Newcastle know how much Guimaraes wants to leave and join Arsenal, and we know the current situation financially from a Newcastle point of view.

"That's one of the reasons Eddie Howe left, he knew Guimaraes would be sold to Arsenal at some point.

"Newcastle want to avoid what happened with Alexander Isak last summer because it didn't bring anything good to anyone - not Newcastle, Isak or Liverpool.

"I expect to see this go through in the next couple of weeks, and from an Arsenal point of view they get not only one of the best midfielders in the Premier League, but someone who can play as a No 6, a No 8 and a No 10.

"The idea from Mikel Arteta to sign him is how press-resistant he is. If you play against a team who come and chase you and want to play out from the back, Bruno is the best at that role.

"I fully expect him to play in front of the back four, and have Rice and Odegaard either side of him, and be able to dictate the tempo and control everything."

Sports.title: Tzolis unfazed by Vini Jr rumours as fitness champion settles into Arsenal
Sports.content:
At Arsenal, there is an excitement about whether Vinicius Jr could sign this summer. But on Saturday, they were given a decent reminder that Christos Tzolis now plays for the club on the left wing.

On his Arsenal debut against Girona, Tzolis strode forward with confidence at his defender, cut inside defiantly and slotted an effort into the bottom corner, via a slight deflection.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Relive Arsenal's 4-1 win over Spanish side Girona in their latest pre-season friendly

Mikel Arteta says the Greek winger is a player that Arsenal fans will love watching and that goal in Catalonia was a positive early sign of that - so how does he feel about Arsenal still attempting to buy a star left winger to play ahead of him?

"Obviously I'm confident as a player, so I don't think about the future and what the club will do in this position," Tzolis responds when asked that question by Sky Sports from Arsenal's pre-season training camp in Spain.

"I'm thinking how to improve and settle as fast as possible in the club because I have the opportunity to train directly with the team from the beginning of the season, to play the friendly games and then to go to official games.

"So it's a chance to play directly from the beginning - and then it's up to me to show the qualities and what I can bring in the team. I'm pretty confident that I will show it in the next games."

Tzolis is speaking in his first interview with reporters since making the £34m move from Club Brugge. After getting 51 goal contributions in 52 games last season, he comes across as direct, honest, polite - but also really driven to succeed at Arsenal.

Image: Tzolis impressed on his Arsenal debut after signing from Club Brugge for £34m

He was in his hometown of Thessaloniki when the call came from his agent that the Premier League champions were interested in him. While other clubs tried to hijack the deal, his mind was set after a few calls with Mikel Arteta.

But while the Arsenal manager is convinced that Tzolis can become a cult hero at Arsenal in the same way the departed Leandro Trossard was, he may need to convince a few fans that he can live up to that mark. So how is he planning to go about that?

"He doesn't want [me] to do things differently than I did in Club Brugge," said Tzolis about his conversations with Arteta.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikel Arteta insists Arsenal are remaining 'ambitious' in the transfer window, as rumours of Real Madrid star Vinicius Junior joining the club intensify

"I think [I need] to be myself and to show on the pitch all the passion and desire to win. Because I really like to win games and to give everything.

"If I give 100 per cent for every game, every duel, who doesn't like this? That's the best thing for a football player and then always you have the support from the fans."

How Tzolis dazzled Arsenal's fitness coaches in pre-season

Direct. Creative. Work Rate. Those are three qualities Tzolis claims are his best attributes in this chat with reporters. But within the Arsenal camp, he is getting plaudits for another reason.

The 24-year-old finished first in one of Arsenal's big pre-season testing challenges - a 1.4km run at full pace. It consists of running 20 metres then back, then the same with 40 metres, then 60 metres, and you do each distance five times in a row.

And these fitness performances has earned Tzolis the nickname 'Leonidas' from one of Arsenal's fitness coaches - after the Gerard Butler character from the film 300.

"There are not all the players here," he says, with a sense of humility. "There are still some players that have to do the tests, of course. But so far I'm first in the fitness test. It's pretty hard.

Image: Tzolis has impressed Arsenal's fitness coaches during pre-season

"I had the advantage that I started pre-season also with Brugge so I was already training for two weeks and always I wanted to keep myself fit during summer so I was ready. I came here ready, my fitness level and I was happy that I could show it here as well."

The Leonidas name is pretty apt for several reasons. One, because he is the direct replacement for another 'Leo' in Trossard, who departed for Besiktas this summer.

But in Ancient Greek history, Leonidas was the famous King of Sparta who led a small Greek force into battle against a massive Persian army.

'Small Greek force' is also a term that can describe Tzolis, especially after hearing Arsenal's new signing goes into detail about how he has moulded his game while looking up to Barcelona and Spain legend David Villa.

"His body style is similar to mine," says Tzolis. "We are not the tallest as strikers but in finishing terms, he was top level.

"I'm not saying I'm the level of David Villa but we have some similarities. He was not a striker, striker. He was an inside forward - a left pocket player who always went for goals.

"I see myself like this because I'm not always a typical wide winger. I go inside a lot and Villa, as a winger/inside forward, was top level."

Another player Tzolis claims he has similarities too is former Arsenal winger Alexis Sanchez, who took on the No 17 shirt when he arrived at Arsenal in 2014. Tzolis has taken that same squad number upon joining the Gunners this year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tzolis attempts to sing the Arsenal anthem and reacts to the new shirt! Pictures courtesy of Arsenal

"Of course, I watched a lot of football and he was a top player for Arsenal as a left winger," says Tzolis. "He's one of the players I looked up to when I was younger. And also I see some similarities with him.

"But it's not the reason I took the No 17. It was more that there were not so many options for the lower numbers, and there was also No 18 and 19 available. I had them in the past, so I didn't want to use them again.

"So, I went for the No 17. It's nice. Alexis Sanchez had No 17 - so I hope I will have the same success."

Can Tzolis help Arsenal defend the title?

Tzolis is joining an Arsenal team who are still chasing history. No Arsenal team has defended the top-flight title since Herbert Chapman led the team to it in the 1930s.

But the Greek winger believes the mentality Arsenal are showing in pre-season is a sign they are ready to defend their crown.

Image: Arsenal are aiming to defend the Premier League title

"For the pre-warming up in the gym to go to training and the intensity and how serious everybody is," he says when asked about the most surprising thing about joining Arsenal.

"From gym exercises to recovery sessions, everyone is demanding and trying to do as best as possible and that shows the high-level standards of this team.

"Even in pre-season, everyone is serious for the friendly games, for the training, for every exercise. Of course you expect it, but I didn't know that before.

"When I see the training, and how hungry every player is for every training drill, that means everybody's ready to compete at the highest level. And when you're a player of Arsenal, you want compete for every title that's possible.

"So, it's not only about the Premier League, it's about all the competitions we are playing for. And I see a clear mindset [from the players] and that everybody is on the same page to win titles here. I have seen that in training, and when you train like that in the game, it makes it even better."

Tzolis knows what it's like to join newly-crowned champions and then lose out on the title the following year. That was what happened when he moved to Club Brugge two seasons ago. So what has he learned?

"To defend a title I think you don't have to think about it," he says. "It's more or less more difficult for the other teams because the pressure is there, not on the team who won the title."

Sports.title: Fukofuka departs Scotland Women head coach role
Sports.content:
Scottish Rugby has announced the departure of women's head coach Sione Fukofuka due to personal reasons after eight months in charge.

Fukofuka joined Scotland in December - shortly before the Women's Six Nations campaign - and led his side to a fifth-place finish, with their only win coming against Wales.

Following Fukofuka's departure, forwards coach Dave Butcher will take interim charge of Scotland ahead of the WXV Global series, beginning September 13.

"I've had to make probably the hardest professional decision of my life to step away from the role as head coach," Fukofuka said.

"I approached Scottish Rugby and asked for a release from my contract under compassionate grounds. Effectively, the stress and the strain on my family, who are back in Australia away from me, proved too much to continue and to do this role the way it should be.

Image: Fukofuka took charge of Scotland Women in December

"With the time back home in Australia over the summer, it was able to give me a lot more insight into the sacrifices that they're making, on top of those that I make as well.

"We also had a change in circumstances where, unfortunately, my wife's parents are unwell, so that means the family relocating in the 12-month plan that we had is not feasible any more.

"I can't be away from my family for that amount of time and do the job the way it should be done."

Scottish Rugby performance director David Nucifora added: "I would like to thank Sione for his contribution to Scottish Rugby and whilst we are disappointed to see him depart, we fully respect and understand the reasons why he has made this decision.

"During his time in the role, Sione showed great passion and commitment to the national team and the wider women's programme at Scottish Rugby.

"Our priority remains supporting the women's national team and women's programme players and staff during this period, with work being done to ensure appropriate structures are in place ahead of the WXV Global Series, along with long-term recruitment conversations."

Sports.title: 'Made of muscles!' Why PSG want Japan goalkeeper Suzuki
Sports.content:
Having been linked with a move to the Premier League, Zion Suzuki is set for a switch to European champions Paris Saint-German instead. It marks the completion of the 23-year-old Japanese goalkeeper's rise to the game's summit after a stellar World Cup.

The eye-catching Suzuki is a phenomenon - as his old goalkeeper coach Dennis Rudel explained when speaking to him last year. "It is like his body is just made of muscles," he told Sky Sports. "And I have never seen in my life a goalkeeper who can jump higher."

Rudel recalled his physical tests being "off the charts" during the player's first season in Europe with Belgian club Sint-Truiden. But Suzuki was identified as a goalkeeper of the future long before that, even when he was warming the bench for Urawa Red Diamonds.

Frans Hoek, the world-famous goalkeeping coach, had been tasked with helping Japan achieve their goal of winning the World Cup by 2050 by revamping their goalkeeper coaching. "We made a pathway for the talented goal players," Hoek told Sky Sports.

The phrase 'goal players' is part of Hoek's insistence that there is more to the job than keeping goal. And he spotted Suzuki. "I saw him in a camp and said, 'this guy has to go to Europe as soon as possible. It does not matter what league it is. He has to play'."

From Sint-Truiden, Suzuki has gone on to spend two seasons in Serie A with Parma before proving to be among the standout goalkeepers at the World Cup. He garnered praise for his efforts against Netherlands before impressing even in defeat to Brazil.

Image: Suzuki tips Vinicius Junior's shot against the post during the World Cup clash with Brazil

One particular stop from Vinicius Junior low to his left was among the saves of the tournament but it has become something of a trademark. For someone with Suzuki's immense frame, he is very capable of extending those long arms low across the ground.

There was a double save against Roma in his debut season with Parma, while Rudel's favourite was one at Club Brugge. "It is those low saves because he is so dynamic and so quick to get down. He has unbelievable reflexes. For me, that is his biggest strength."

Something special in those fingertips? "With those low power saves, his arms are so strong. Sometimes when goalkeepers go down fast and get their fingers to the ball, it still goes backwards. That never happens to him. He has crazy power in his hands."

Image: Japan goalkeeper Suzuki catches the ball during the World Cup game against Brazil

There is a story that illustrates this perfectly. Rudel was setting up a drill during one of their first sessions together. "I said to him, 'okay, now show me how far you can throw'. I looked away and then saw this ball flying 20 metres over the halfway line," he recalled.

"I turned around and said, 'I told you to throw it not kick it'. He just smiled back at me and replied, 'but I did throw it'. I told him to show me again because I could not believe that someone had that much power in their body that they could throw the ball that far."

It hints at the combination of skills that makes Suzuki so unusual. As well as those low saves, he ranks second in Serie A for high claims last season. In the previous campaign, only Barcelona goalkeeper Joan Garcia claimed more crosses in Europe's top leagues.

Image: Suzuki's per-90 stats for Parma during the 2025/26 Serie A season

Suzuki was second in Serie A for successful long passes last season but he also ranked highly for sweeping up behind the defence and saving shots. There will be less of that required in Paris than Parma but Rudel believes Suzuki's temperament is an asset too.

Despite describing him as "really aggressive because he has massive physical strength - he is so powerful, so dynamic" on the pitch, he is a very different person away from it. "He is a really quiet guy, a really calm character. That is him off the pitch," added Rudel.

There have been difficult moments to overcome along the way. Errors in the 2023 Asian Cup, when he was still just 21, were followed by vile racist abuse. Now, Suzuki is a national hero and his status is only going to rise with a move to the reigning champions of Europe.

Born in New York to a Ghanaian-American father, Suzuki is as Japanese as they come, having grown up in the country. "That culture is totally his." Paris Syndrome is an infamous issue for Japanese people overwhelmed by the city. Suzuki will be fine.

Asked if he could reach the top, Rudel replied: "One hundred per cent. That is another of his strengths. He went from Japan to Belgium and then Belgium to Italy. Those are big adaptations but he did it really quickly. That is what separates the really good ones."

Suzuki might still need to be patient, even go out on loan before claiming the No 1 shirt for himself. But this is a move that takes him a step closer to fulfilling the potential that Rudel and Hoek identified many years ago. PSG have their goalkeeper of the future.

Sports.title: English FA to drop support for Gianni Infantino after Wales withdraw backing
Sports.content:
The Football Association will formally withdraw its support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as the Fifa president, adding to the mounting pressure on his crisis-hit tenure. In a significant development, the FA will write to Fifa confirming it no longer backs Infantino for a fourth term in charge, having previously offered its endorsement. Their move comes after the Welsh FA dropped its backing for Infantino’s candidature.

More European countries are expected to follow suit in an attempt to force his resignation. The Football Association of Finland became the first country to withdraw its support last week.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Guardian reported on Sunday that Uefa federations have been preparing a mass withdrawal of letters supporting Infantino. All bar five of the continent’s 55 member associations had communicated their backing before last week’s revelation of his privately backed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup.

The FA has previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the UK’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday, it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation.

While the FA’s stance is robust, it is not expected to publicise its withdrawal letter due to a view, also held in some other parts of Europe, that the movement to unseat Infantino needs to gather momentum on different continents. Opposition within Europe will not be difficult to achieve, but Infantino’s future may hinge on the degree of leadership taken by members of the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, where opinion on his reign has been more divided.

The Football Association of Wales confirmed on Monday morning that it no longer supports Infantino. “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino, for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027–2031 term,” it said.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

Welsh football and its representatives have played a key role in moves to oppose Infantino. In a meeting of member associations last Thursday, Laura McAllister, a Uefa vice-president and former Wales international, advocated a Europe-led boycott of Fifa competitions if Infantino did not scrap the FFE scheme. It led to a collective agreement that effectively rendered the plan untenable.

Sports.title: Marc Skinner leaves Manchester United Women head coach role amid transfer frustration
Sports.content:
Marc Skinner has left his role as Manchester United’s head coach by mutual consent after five years, partly because of the club’s transfer strategy. The 43-year-old is understood to have initiated the discussions that led to his departure, having felt it was the right time to leave the club. United are focusing on developing young players, rather than enter into bidding wars with some of the Women’s Super League’s bigger spenders.

The former Birmingham and Orlando head coach led Manchester United to three consecutive Women’s FA Cup finals between 2023 and 2025, winning one – and the club’s first major women’s trophy – in 2024 at Wembley with a 4-0 victory over . His side also reached the quarter-finals of the Women’s Champions League in 2025-26, as well as the League Cup final.

Skinner has repeatedly called for greater investment in the team in the transfer market and a change in strategy from the club this summerhas led to his exit.

Skinner oversaw a second-placed finish in the 2022-23 campaign, the club’s highest league position, after a fourth-placed finish in his first season in charge, in 2021-22. United then finished fifth, third and fourth respectively in his final three years in charge.

Sources have indicated the women’s team has a new direction this summer, focused on building a team sustainably with homegrown players, which the club are understood to feel fits their identity of developing youth. Investments are being made into United’s academy.

But other sources have said Skinner was increasingly frustrated at seeing WSL sides outspend United. The sale of French striker Melvine Malard to Chelsea, for a club-record fee in the region of £850,000, has caused concern about the club’s ambition for the upcoming season.

View image in fullscreen Melvine Malard (left) left Manchester United in a club-record sale to Chelsea. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

It comes while London City Lionesses – United’s opponents on the season’s opening day on 4 September – have spent significantly on Spain’s Alexia Putellas and Mapi León, as well as France winger Kadidiatou Diani.

Sources close to the club have indicated they feel such spending is not sustainable in the women’s game. Ultimately, discussions around these matters have concluded with the club and Skinner parting ways before a new campaign when the team can make a fresh start.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Since it became clear Skinner would be leaving, the club have a shortlist of candidates and they are expected to name his replacement relatively quickly.

“Marc leaves having made a significant contribution to the continued progress of Manchester United Women,” United said. “The club places on record its sincere thanks for his professionalism, commitment and dedication throughout his time at United, and wishes him every success in the future.”

Sports.title: Worn in the USA: Liverpool’s pre-season tour had highs but exposed glaring gaps in the squad | Andy Hunter
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola’s first pre-season tour as the Liverpool head coach produced wins over Sunderland in Nashville and Wrexham in New York before ending in a 4-2 defeat against Leeds in Chicago. The Guardian followed the tour throughout and here are a few things we learned.

Iraola’s vision for Liverpool will take time

Liverpool’s second-half display against Leeds was both concerning and valuable for the Iraola as set-piece problems and a tendency to switch off – two of last season’s recurring themes – reared their ugly head again, albeit after he had made changes. Liverpool’s opening 45 minutes, however, was their best of the tour and showed how effective his front-foot, more intense style can be with the big names back. But that process is only just under way.

Iraola is yet to even meet Virgil van Dijk, Cody Gakpo, Alisson, Alexis Mac Allister and new signing Víctor Muñoz since his appointment almost two months ago, never mind coach them. They will be finally be acquainted when the squad reports back for training on Wednesday, having been given a little time off to recover from Sunday night’s flight from Chicago. Mac Allister will be still absent after his World Cup exertions. There is less than three weeks to go and only two more friendlies (although it is a double-header against Como at Anfield) before Liverpool open their Premier League season at Newcastle. “I would like to say on the first day we are going to be perfect, everyone will be in place,” Iraola said. “But probably it is not going to be like this.”

New head coach needs more backing

For most of the tour, Iraola was without eight first-team players due to World-Cup holidays and six because of injury, either recovering from or, as in the unfortunate Joe Gomez’s case, sustained in the US. No prizes for stating that Liverpool’s performances and adaptation to Iraola’s methods would have been much more advanced with 14 extra first-team players available. Even so, glaring gaps remain in the team when every option is taken into account.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool knew about Mohamed Salah’s departure months ago, but have yet to line up a replacement. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

Mohamed Salah’s departure was announced in March. Talks to end his contract one year early commenced earlier. Five months on from the announcement, he is yet to be replaced. The seriousness of Conor Bradley’s knee injury means Liverpool remain light at right-back. There are the highest hopes for Jérémy Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni – the latter has transformed himself into a strapping Adonis while recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury, by the way – while 18-year-olds Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye did well in the US. But Liverpool are lacking Premier League experience in central defence and Ndukwe will be unable to play this season due to post-Brexit work permit difficulties. Gomez’s injury record means he must be considered a bonus when fit, rather than one of four options. It was interesting to hear Iraola explain how he likes wingers to play both flanks, and the advantages of switching them during a game, but Liverpool’s right side could be a problem even if they succeed in signing Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain.

View image in fullscreen Trey Nyoni’s confident and assured displays pressed his case for more Liverpool game time. Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty Images

Nyoni is now firmly in Iraola’s plans

There was an enforced reliance on young players during the tour and Iraola was genuinely impressed by the levels many showed in training and the friendlies. Ndukwe and Talla Ndiaye, as mentioned, Lewis Koumas, Kieran Morrison and Luke Chambers were among them. But no prospect pushed their first team claims further than Nyoni, who grew in stature and confidence with every outing. The 19-year-old and Rio Ngumoha were permanent fixtures in Arne Slot’s squad last season, but while the winger made 19 appearances in the Premier League, including five starts, Nyoni had to settle for six league outings from the bench. On this evidence, there will be many more this season. The midfielder looked immediately at ease with Iraola’s instructions to find forward options as quickly as possible and did so whether under pressure or by creating space for himself with intelligent movement. His pass in the buildup to Florian Wirtz’s goal against Leeds was exquisite and in keeping with his contribution overall. Nyoni said after the Leeds game he knew he had to improve this summer. He was as good as his word.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Jones did not seize chance to impress

To pinch a phrase from Salah, Jones looked more out than in at times as he enters the final 12 months of his Liverpool contract with increasing interest from the Italian champions, Inter. Unlike Nyoni and Dominik Szoboszlai, the 25-year-old did not adapt comfortably to Iraola’s requirements for a central midfielder and particularly struggled when introduced in the second half against Leeds. But it was his petulant reaction to not receiving the captain’s armband from Szoboszlai against Wrexham that did him fewest favours.

Jones was also overlooked for the captaincy when Gomez exited the opening game against Sunderland. On both occasions the armband was passed to Kostas Tsimikas, a reserve left-back who spent last season on loan at Roma. Of course, that was going to annoy a boyhood Liverpool fan and one of the more senior players on the tour, and Jones, Szoboszlai and Tsimikas all went to great lengths to laugh off the incident in the days after the Wrexham win. The row might have been overblown on social media, but given Iraola stresses the importance of the collective, Jones’s individualistic behaviour jarred with what he is trying to build.

View image in fullscreen Dominik Szoboszlai led the way for Liverpool on the US tour. Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty Images

Szoboszlai wins popularity contest

In the absence of Salah, Andy Robertson, Van Dijk and Alisson, and in keeping with his status as Liverpool’s player of last season, Szoboszlai was undoubtedly the big attraction for fans in the US. The Hungary captain’s every introduction and contribution was met with fanatical acclaim and his was the face the media wanted on their channels. More importantly for Iraola, Szoboszlai led the way in training and his leadership was invaluable given the relative inexperience of the squad. Fresh from signing a new five-year contract, the 25-year-old is an obvious choice to fill one of the vice-captain vacancies created by the departures of Salah and Robertson.

Sports.title: On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time
Sports.content:
It is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Totti dusted it off for the internet generation at Euro 2000.

It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means. The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.

A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder. Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards, asked the man himself what constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible. Rob Smyth

View image in fullscreen The man himself, pictured earlier this year. Photograph: Björn Steinz/The Guardian

Antonin Panenka, 1976

Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)

This one needs no introduction. RS

Antonin Panenka, 1979

Czechoslovakia 2-0 France

The next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsy with a sensual chip in a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80. RS

Diego Maradona, 1984

Napoli training

Most of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner to ensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d already seen him do it in open play. RS

Eric Cantona, 1989

Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)

In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackle of comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowd and tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot, he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset. Daniel Harris

Gianluca Vialli, 1990

Monaco 2-2 Sampdoria

In the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure: against Genoa in the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90. The first was against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16, the second in the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0 in the final. RS

Michal Bilek, 1990

Czechoslovakia 5-1 USA

It’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976. He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!” RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

Nottingham Forest 1-1 Tottenham

Nobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led to a brief post-match discussion in which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. This one was particularly sweet – the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final. RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

England 1-1 Brazil

A kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearer chuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak, as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record. Jonathan Liew

View image in fullscreen With a share of England’s goalscoring record for the taking, Gary Lineker dinks tamely into the arms of the Brazil goalkeeper Carlos. Illustration: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images

Eric Cantona, 1994

Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)

In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final, he’d gently rolled two penalties into the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the way only for the kick to sail over the bar as United lost 6-5. DH

Djalminha, 1995

Guarani 2-1 Internacional

Brazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for his signature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot. The first of many was scored against Sergio Goycoechea, whose elastic penalty saves had taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1996

Sheffield United 0-1 Aston Villa

Dwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule, but Yorke was true to his word and settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.” RS

Gianluca Vialli, 1996

Chelsea 2-4 Wimbledon

There’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. But Vialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line by a very different kind of chip earlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1998

Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal

“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman, who was Panenka-ed on the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called, Yorke sidefooted wide. RS

John Eyre, 1999

Torquay 0-1 Hull City

If only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue as this piece of effrontery floated gently past him. RS

Francesco Totti, 2000

Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)

In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti, whose falling leaf penalty foxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation. John Brewin

View image in fullscreen Francesco Totti brings the Panenka into the 21st century. Illustration: Henri Szwarc/Bongarts/Getty Images

Mixu Paatelainen, 2001

Hibernian 0-0 Hearts

A last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares. Mixu Paatelainen only took it because Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion. RS

Thierry Henry, 2003

Arsenal 3-2 Newcastle

Five days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner was teased softly down the middle by Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was just trolling Ruud van Nistelrooy. RS

View image in fullscreen Thierry Henry went full va-va-voom for his winning penalty against Newcastle. Illustration: Jamie McDonald/Getty Images

Mickaël Landreau, 2004

Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)

For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka. Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chanceto secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup. Jeff Rueter

Liam Lawrence, 2004

Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)

Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). On the Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.

double quotation mark LL I’m gonna dink it. BH No you’re not. LL I am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final. BH Liam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.

He dinked that ball against the bar – “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.” RS

Helder Postiga, 2004

Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)

Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty, a kick so under-amped it barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp. JB

Peter Crouch, 2006

England 6-0 Jamaica

The then-Liverpool striker scored an England hat-trick as part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ball well over the bar from 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.” Will Unwin

View image in fullscreen Judging by his expression, Peter Crouch knew he’d got his penalty wrong as soon as he hit it. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Artem Milevskiy, 2006

Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)

You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it came after 120 minutes of the most soporific football ever played. RS

Zinedine Zidane, 2006

Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)

The nerve to do it in a World Cup final. The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar, past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – until Marco Materazzi and the anger took over. Taha Hashim

View image in fullscreen Zinedine Zidane steps up… Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen … and beats Gianluigi Buffon all ends up. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Archive/PA Images

Yann Kermogant, 2010

Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)

To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier, dollied his kick into the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even has his own Bonnie Tyler adaptation. JB

Sebastián Abreu, 2010

Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)

If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one of the first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup. A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions. RS

Andrea Pirlo, 2012

England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)

When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ball wafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successes finishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards. DH

View image in fullscreen Andrea Pirlo icily dinks his penalty over a fired-up Joe Hart. Illustration: Matthias Schräder/AP

Sergio Ramos, 2012

Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)

For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-final against Portugal. Bruno Alves missed Portugal’s next kick and Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final. RS

Maicosuel, 2012

Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)

The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenka was saved in a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.” RS

Graziano Pellè, 2012

SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)

Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpah to try a Pellènka? RS

Rogério Ceni, 2013

São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)

No surprise that one of the great goalscoring keepers should beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he was fractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically. RS

Alexandre Pato, 2013

Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)

Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to take one of the worst Panenkas ever seen. RS

Alexis Sánchez, 2015

Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)

It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone. His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – and unlike Czechoslovakia in 1976, they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria. RS

Aaron Ramsey, 2017

Serbia 1-1 Wales

The Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramsey unwittingly did so by scoring a Panenka at the same end of the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one. RS

View image in fullscreen Aaron Ramsey does a Panenka more completely than most. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Reuters

George Calintaru, 2017

Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua Bucuresti

A Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger. RS

Fedor Smolov, 2018

Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)

Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend that Fedor Smolov’s opening attempt lacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour. JR

Lionel Messi, 2020

Barcelona 2-2 Atlético Madrid

If you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium, you might as well do it in style. RS

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi’s penalty record is suprisingly human, but he got the one that gave him his 700th goal right. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

Fara Williams, 2020

Reading 3-1 Aston Villa

This unusual penalty from Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority. RS

Ademola Lookman, 2020

West Ham 1-0 Fulham

During his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the game but his feeble chip landed straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare moment of post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.” Yara El-Shaboury

Santi Cazorla, 2021

Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al Sadd

Not many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right foot against Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021. RS

Sergio Agüero, 2021

Man City 1-2 Chelsea

City were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided to chip down the middle; Édouard Mendy almost fell for it but had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüero issued a public apology. WU

View image in fullscreen Sergio Agüero’s Panenka attempt almost, but crucially only almost, fools Édouard Mendy. Photograph: Shaun Botterill/AFP/Getty Images

Marta, 2022

France 2-1 Brazil

Birthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against France in sublime fashion.JR

Karim Benzema, 2022

Manchester City 4-3 Real Madrid

A moment of mischief at the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final. RS

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s improbable run to winning the 2022 Champions League included Karim Benzema coming up clutch – again. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Achraf Hakimi, 2022

Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)

If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final, you might as well do it in style. RS

Gaëtane Thiney, 2023

Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FC

We can’t say for sure that this is the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition. RS

Antoine Mille, 2024

Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)

In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after saving one of the more pitiful Panenkas ever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille. RS

Marta, 2025

Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego Wave

If you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025, chipping in off the underside of the crossbar to secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill. Tom Garry

Alexia Putellas, 2025

Roma 0-4 Barcelona

Even the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenka harmlessly over the crossbar during a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner. TG

Tiaguinho, 2025

Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)

A Panenka is a dish best served cold. RS

Brahim Díaz, 2026

Morocco 3-0* Senegal

Brahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenka was easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding. Then again … YE-S

View image in fullscreen Brahim Díaz’s miss saw Morocco squander their chance to win the Afcon. Or so we thought… Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Mohamed Salah, 2026

Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)

Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is that Mo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australia was the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream. RS

Sports.title: ‘It’s my time’: Christos Tzolis fighting fit for Arsenal on return to England
Sports.content:
For any Arsenal fan eager to know what Christos Tzolis might bring to the Premier League champions, the winger’s swiftly earned nickname at his new club might prove instructive. In the 2006 action film 300, the leading figure of King Leonidas guides a meagre bunch of Spartans against an overwhelmingly large invading army. Although doomed by the vast numerical disadvantage, Leonidas’s courage, determination and strength inspires his troops far beyond their means. It is his name that Arsenal’s fitness coaches have given their new Greek.

Within a week of his £34m move from Club Brugge, Tzolis had made himself conspicuous at Arsenal’s training ground by acing a host of pre-season tests, topping the charts in one particular fitness challenge that involves players running more than a kilometre over varying intervals. Modesty forbids him from revealing the remainder of his physical results but, with a smile, he concedes they were “good”.

Tzolis has been here before, albeit in vastly different circumstances. The last time he played Premier League football he was a teenager, starting three times for a Norwich side that finished bottom in 2021-22. The following campaign he started only three Championship games after an unsuccessful loan spell at the Dutch club Twente. When he headed on loan again, to Fortuna Düsseldorf, his time in East Anglia was over. But it was in Germany’s second tier that his trajectory shifted.

“In football it’s not always going up. You can have some setbacks and difficulties,” says Tzolis. “I learned a lot of things from this period at Norwich. That’s why I wanted to go to Düsseldorf to get the confidence back, because I knew I have the skills and qualities to score goals.

“Even though it was not the highest level, like playing in the Premier League, it’s good to play every game and have the feeling that you can score and create, and play good games. Then you go to the next level, which is Club Brugge, and I had two amazing years there because I made the decision to go to Düsseldorf and have the confidence.

“I feel now more ready to be in the Premier League. For me, I did the right decision after Norwich. I developed myself, I improved a lot. I’m not the same player I was in Norwich, 100%. I feel it in my body and also in my mindset. Now it’s my time to show that I’m ready and capable of playing in the Premier League.” It is a thoughtful explanation from a thoughtful man; someone who says he is eager to absorb the wealth of cultures within a football dressing room.

Tzolis’ bare numbers from Belgium certainly support his assertion of improvement. In two seasons at Club Brugge, he scored 33 goals. His spectacular 2025-26 campaign caught Arsenal’s eye, with 17 goals and 23 assists – 16 more goal involvements than any other player in the league – to help his side regain the title.

View image in fullscreen Christos Tzolis scored his first Arsenal goal in the friendly win against Girona on Saturday. Photograph: Agencia LOF/Action Plus/Shutterstock

Life at Belgium’s dominant force was far removed from the difficult task that had presented itself at Norwich, where Tzolis made his Premier League debut at Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium he will now call home. “The team was not ready for the Premier League and that makes it also difficult for me to adapt and to play how I could play,” he says. “I’m a more offensive player, and a player that plays for a team that has the ball and creates a lot of chances. With Norwich we had to defend more low and maybe to have some transition moments, but that was not working. Obviously the game time was not enough as a young player to develop and that was the bad thing of the Norwich situation.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tzolis was enjoying this summer in his home town of Thessaloniki when first informed of Arsenal’s desire to sign him as a replacement for Leandro Trossard on the left flank. He had two long conversations with Mikel Arteta, who informed Tzolis that he should do nothing different to that which lit up the Belgian Pro League. “It’s always difficult to say no to Arsenal,” says the Greece international. “There were some teams that talked and asked, but not concrete. Arsenal was directly the most concrete team and that made it easier for me to lock in and to say: ‘I want just to go there, I don’t want to hear anything else.’ It was an easy choice.”

Tzolis models his game on the Spanish great David Villa – “a left-pocket player who always went for goals” – and his first pre-season goal, in a 4-1 win against Girona on Saturday, arrived in precisely that fashion; cutting inside and curling the ball inside the far post.

Tzolis prides himself on his “passion and desire to win”, adding that he intends to “give 100% for every game, every duel”. Leonidas would demand nothing less.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Atlético to offer Grealish escape route? Spurs target Osimhen and Gakpo?
Sports.content:
Jack Grealish needs a route out of Manchester City and could be offered one by Atlético Madrid. Everton, where he spent last season on loan, and first club Aston Villa are also lurking as the winger recovers from injury. The 30-year-old is absent from City’s pre-season tour and his future at the Etihad Stadium does not have a positive outlook, even after Enzo Maresca replaced Pep Guardiola.

Tottenham’s attempts to add some more attacking power has caused them to enquire about Galatasaray’s Victor Osimhen and Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo, not that either would come cheaply. One imminent outgoing is the youngster Mikey Moore who is closing on a loan move to Cologne.

Manchester United need more options at left-back than just Luke Shaw. The defender showed he can survive a full season without European complications but with plenty more matches in the offing, adding strength in depth is a priority. This publication has suggested Newcastle’s Lewis Hall is a potential target and Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly is another on the radar.

Juventus are exploring the possibility of signing the Tottenham goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario on loan. The Italian side are looking for a new No 1 and Vicario is understood to want to return home. The ramped up interest may relate to their pursuit of Aston Villa’s Emiliano Martínez being over, while fellow target Zion Suzuki is set to leave Parma for Paris Saint-Germain.

Things are ramping up in Hull as they look to get some deals done after missing out on Burnley’s Florentino Luis, who is on his way to Ipswich. Australia’s teenage sensation Lucas Herrington is close to be becoming a Tiger after talks between the Premier League side and Colorado Rapids. Meanwhile, the newly-promoted club are working away at bringing Leon Bailey from Aston Villa and Tim Iroegbunam from Everton.

If Bournemouth were hoping to focus on incomings, then Al-Hilal may throw a curveball into the mix by bidding for Rayan. One has to suspect that it would take an incredible offer for either the club or player to even contemplate progressing with the idea. The good news for the Cherries is that the right-back Juanlu Sánchez is on his way to the south coast after Sevilla agreed to sell him for £9.5m plus add-ons.

Relegation and selling off most of one’s assets eventually results in having to sign some players to inspire a new era. For West Ham – and their new minority ownership – AZ’s Troy Parrott is the first possible brick in the rebuild, but they face competition from Real Betis and Ajax. Fulham are also reportedly keen on the Republic of Ireland striker.

Mohamed Salah knows how to create drama on the pitch but could be set to orchestrate some off it. Whispers suggest the former Liverpool forward is about to join Trabzonspor despite reportedly discussing with Besiktas that he would head to Istanbul on a free. The lure of playing alongside John Lundstram seemingly knows no bounds.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Down in League One, Leicester are interested in Millwall’s Luke Cundle, who previously worked with Russell Martin at Swansea. And the Luton forward Lasse Nordås has rejected a number of offers from abroad because he is eager to stay in England. He’s turned down moves to Rakow Czestochowa, Heerenveen, Samsunspor and two clubs in Scandinavia.

Sports.title: Chelsea sign Argentina international Valentín Barco from Strasbourg
Sports.content:
Chelsea have signed the Argentina international Valentín Barco from their sister club Strasbourg on a seven-year deal.

The 22-year-old, who played seven times for Brighton including six Premier League appearances during the 2023-24 season, becomes the eighth arrival of new manager Xabi Alonso’s reign.

A versatile player who can be used in central midfield as well as his regular position of left-back, Barco was in the Argentina squad that finished as runners-up at the World Cup, winning his fifth cap in the 3-1 group-stage win over Jordan.

He moved to Strasbourg initially on loan from Brighton in 2025 and signed permanently later that year having helped the club to qualify for the Conference League. In all he made 54 appearances for the Ligue 1 side.

He was involved in a heated exchange with England’s Jude Bellingham immediately after his side’s 2-1 World Cup semi-final win in Atlanta, with Bellingham appearing to clip Barco around the head. The Argentinian, who was an unused substitute, had earlier run on to the pitch to celebrate after Enzo Fernández had equalised. He is expected to join up shortly with his new teammates on their tour of Australia and Hong Kong.

It continues a busy summer in the transfer market for Chelsea as they look to remodel under Alonso. On Saturday they confirmed the signing of the veteran striker Danny Welbeck from Brighton, following the signings of Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa. Denner, Marco Palestra, Emmanuel Emegha and Geovany Quenda have also been signed.

Sports.title: Socceroos on the move: Herrington headlines post-World Cup transfers
Sports.content:
Lucas Herrington, fresh off becoming the youngest Australian to start a game at a men’s World Cup, is set to become the second-most expensive footballer in Australian history with a move to newly-promoted Premier League side Hull City. Latest reports suggest a fee of approximately £12.6m ($24.1m), with a further £4.4m ($8.4m) in add-ons, which comes in just shy of the Australian record of £15m plus £5m in add-ons ($38.3m in total) that Leicester paid Stoke City to sign Harry Souttar in 2023.

It would set a new selling high-water mark for his current club, Colorado Rapids, and eclipses the decade-old record Hull set when they paid just over £10m for Ryan Mason. Given the trajectory of Herrington’s meteoric rise, it feels a pretty safe bet to assume the 18-year-old will claim Souttar’s record outright sooner rather than later.

Hull may not be quite as attractive as a move to Barcelona or Liverpool, both of whom were linked to Herrington in recent months. But such a view overlooks that it was only a few years ago that a lack of representation in major European leagues was decried. Clubs in those competitions are now paying record fees for Australia’s brightest young talents.

The only cohort in Australia that should be perturbed by the deal is those connected to Brisbane Roar, having watched as the club (which as a reminder, is granted a monopoly over Queensland by the A-League Men’s current closed nature) sold their sell-on fee back to the Rapids for a reported $560,000. It meant the club missed out on a minimum $4.8m, not even a year on from Herrington’s departure.

Importantly, in moving to Hull’s MKM Stadium rather than the Camp Nou or Anfield for such a significant fee, the central defender should ostensibly be able to play the regular senior football that will maintain his remarkable rise. Even if Hull prove to be one-and-done in the English top-flight, Herrington will still be a teenager at the end of this season, battle-hardened by a year of playing on club football’s biggest stage on his resume.

Barring disaster, it should only help establish his future at that level, as well as help develop his game in a manner in which the Socceroos can reap the benefits.

Herrington is not the only member of the young cohort from Tony Popovic’s Socceroos squad that looks set to capitalise on appearing at the World Cup, even if the days of the tournament serving as a one-stop shop for the transfer market have long since passed. In the days of modern analytics and digitised global scouting, no player is ever truly off the radar.

Herrington is one of eight players aged 23 or under who started a game in North America. Since the tournament ended, Paul-Okon Engstler sealed a move from Sydney FC to Bundesliga outfit FC Köln, while breakout goalkeeper Patrick Beach concluded a move seven months in the making when he shifted in the City Football Group from Melbourne City to newly-promoted Ligue 1 side Troyes.

View image in fullscreen Paul Okon-Engstler appears in a pre-season friendly for his new club FC Köln. Photograph: Marco Steinbrenner/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

The moves of Okon-Engstler and Beach are notable in that they are making the jump straight from the A-League Men to one of Europe’s big five leagues, with early indications from pre-season suggesting they’re chances to start or see decent minutes. Is it remarkable, given the last time Australian players successfully went directly from the Australian top-flight to regular minutes in one of these leagues was in the days of Vince Grella and Stan Lazaridis – who left NSL sides Carlton and West Adelaide, respectively.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There is still plenty of development ahead for the likes of Herrington, Beach and Okon-Engstler. Simply getting to these leagues isn’t the end of the journey, but the start of a new one. But add to this Champions League-bound Sporting CP’s reported pursuit of Nestory Irankunda (on a deal that should eclipse Souttar’s if it goes through) and the Premier League clubs that were circling Jordy Bos before his unfortunate injury against Egypt forced him to undergo surgery, and it substantiates the excitement around the young talent coming through Australian football’s pathways.

And though not of the same age cohort, a strong World Cup also has Souttar, still the Socceroos rock, on the verge of a Championship move, with Sheffield United and Wrexham his reported suitors in a move that should give him much-needed stability and hopes of a promotion push.

Mathew Ryan, after playing a major role in staving off relegation last season, has inked a return to La Liga side Levante for the 2026-27 campaign. In a significant boost to his chances of staying in the Socceroos mix, Tete Yengi has secured a permanent move to J-League side Machida Zelvia after spending the end of last season on loan, while Cammy Devlin has followed Derek McInnes from Hearts to Rangers. Ajdin Hrustić, meanwhile, has moved to UAE outfit Al-Nasr.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes back with Manchester United after World Cup - but club remain in the dark over fitness of striker Benjamin Sesko
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes back with Manchester United after World Cup - but club remain in the dark over fitness of striker Benjamin Sesko

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes is among the latest World Cup contingent to report back to the club’s Carrington headquarters for pre-season training as Michael Carrick’s squad nears full strength.

Fernandes has returned along with his Portugal teammate Diogo Dalot and Brazil’s Matheus Cunha after reaching the last 16, while Noussair Mazraoui is also back after making it to the quarter-finals with Morocco.

The four players will have individual testing and fitness assessment in the first couple of days, and could be in the travelling squad for United’s next pre-season friendly against Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg on Saturday. There, Belgian duo Senne Lammens and new £35million signing Youri Tielemans may also feature after returning to training last week.

It’s unclear if Benjamin Sesko will be able to play after missing United’s first three pre-season games against Wrexham, Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid with an ongoing shin problem, although there could be an update on the Slovenia striker later on Monday.

The last group back will be England duo Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford, plus Lisandro Martinez of Argentina, who are expected to join up with the club’s training camp in Ireland where United will also play Leeds in Dublin.

The club are not expecting any issues with the thigh injury Martinez suffered before half-time in Argentina’s defeat to Spain in the World Cup final, or the back complaint that kept Mainoo out of England’s win over France in the bronze medal match, but are waiting to assess both players once they return.

BrunO Fernandes has returned to training with Manchester United after his summer break

Speaking before United beat Atletico 2-1 in Stockholm on Saturday, Carrick said: ‘We’ve got five or six coming back on Monday, and then more a week after that. The further you get in the World Cup, the less time you have off. We had a bit of a joke about that with the players before they left, that's just how it is.’

Meanwhile, Manuel Ugarte has been undergoing rehab since returning to Carrington in mid-July following surgery on the knee ligament injury he suffered in Uruguay’s group defeat to Spain.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino begs Trump for help as he fights to save his job: 'Isolated' FIFA president 'set for White House talks' after failed bid to sell World Cup
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino begs Trump for help as he fights to save his job: 'Isolated' FIFA president 'set for White House talks' after failed bid to sell World Cup

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Embattled FIFA president Gianni Infantino is reportedly set for crunch talks with the White House on Monday morning as he battles to save his job in the wake of his failed bid to sell off the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino sparked an open revolt when The Times first revealed his bombshell plans to sell a $4.2 billion (£3.1bn) stake in FIFA's flagship tournament to a private equity firm led by Joshua Kushner.

The proposals have since been scrapped after opposition from UEFA, the North, Central America and Caribbean confederation (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

And as Infantino battles to save his job, the New York Post has revealed that Infantino is now turning to his biggest ally - Donald Trump - to help him survive.

The paper reports that Infantino will hold a call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 9am EST (2pm BST), as pressure rises on the FIFA president to resign from his role.

An insider told the Post: 'He wanted to get online with the secretary and talk about how soccer can be a form of soft power for America. But we all know that it is about job protection. It is not about anything else at this point.'

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino is in a fight to save his job after his failed bid to sell the World Cup

Infantino will reportedly hold a call with Marco Rubio (C) on Monday to ask for support

A second source described Infantino as feeling 'isolated' by the 'avalanche' of negativity surrounding his now-doomed plans. 'He is looking for allies of note to publicly support him,' they said.

The Daily Mail has reached out to FIFA and the White House for comment.

Infantino's reported last-ditch attempt to save his presidency comes just days after Trump brutally denied all knowledge of Infantino's bold sell-off plan.

When asked 'did Mr Infantino speak to you about his proposal to sell a stake in the World Cup?' Trump brutally first replied: 'Who?'

After the question was repeated, the president then added: 'No, I didn't speak to him.'

Trump's reaction to Infantino in that Oval Office media session was a far cry from previous comments before and during the World Cup, in which he often gave a glowing review of the FIFA boss.

The Post also reports that Infantino has repeatedly tried to call Trump in the past few days, only to be met with a wall of silence from the president.

Trump brutally responded 'who?' when asked if Infantino had consulted him about his plan

Earlier on Monday, Infantino's battle to survive as FIFA president took another big hit as more nations withdrew their support for his re-election bid.

England, Wales and Finland are the latest countries to explicitly stand against Infantino's re-election, with more UEFA nations expected to follow.

Prior to his controversial sell-off plans, Infantino had reportedly been endorsed by almost all of FIFA's 211 member associations for re-election. Candidates must be put forward by November 18 and the vote will take place at FIFA's congress in March.

Infantino has been FIFA president since 2016 after replacing Sepp Blatter and is targeting a fourth term in charge.

But the events of recent days - and the controversies that blighted him before and during the World Cup - have rocked his authority.

His plans have been widely lambasted and two of his closest allies have resigned. Firstly, his senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro - who acted as FIFA's link to the White House during the tournament - stepped down, before chief operating officer Kevin Lamour lambasted the proposals.

UEFA and CONCACAF have called on Infantino to quit but their ploy to depose the Swiss football administrator hit a roadblock after Kuwait, Qatar, Sri Lanka and Lebanon reiterated their confidence in his leadership.

Joshua Kushner - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law - was at the heart of the plans

A lot has changed since Trump and Infantino handed Spain the World Cup trophy on July 19

UEFA and CONCACAF make up 90 of FIFA's 211 member associations. Although that is above the 20 per cent threshold to trigger a vote of no confidence, it falls short of the majority needed to topple Infantino.

With Infantino retaining support from Africa while South America are expected to take the same position, AFC members would be required to oust the FIFA president.

New Zealand could join Europe and CONCACAF's resistance, but it is doubtful that the remaining 10 members of the Oceania Football Confederation would follow suit.

Infantino wrote to all FIFA nations claiming they would receive $41m (£30m) if they backed his plan to sell off stakes in FIFA's major competitions.
