Sports.title: Emma Raducanu practises in an orthopedic boot as injury-stricken British No 1 unwinds in the Swiss Alps with less than a month to go until US Open
Sports.content:
Emma Raducanu heralded the 'best reset ever' after a holiday in the Swiss Alps, but raised concern among her fans as she continued to practise in an orthopedic boot with less than a month to go until the US Open.

The British No1's season has been one of promising peaks but speckled with injury, after a post-viral illness torpedoed her clay season.

Returning to her stronger grass surface, Raducanu reached the final at Queen's Club before her narrow defeat to Donna Vekic.

The 23-year-old was unable to build on this however, after picking up a grade-four stress fracture in the aftermath of the final which kept her out of Wimbledon.

Raducanu was pictured sporting the protective boot as her WTA peers played their opening rounds in SW19, and shared on social media that she continues to wear it for practising her serve.

The former US Open champion chose the picturesque backdrop of St Moritz's Grand Hotel Suvretta House, a five-star hotel in the heart of the upscale Swiss resort.

Emma Raducanu has been unwinding at the five-star Grand Hotel Suvretta House in St Moritz

The British No 1 continued to practice in an orthopedic boot after sustaining a grade four stress fracture (pictured right in July)

Billed as a 'luxury fitness retreat', the hotel - where a Junior Suite can be booked for £1,038 a-night (1,130 CHF) - boasts tennis courts, a spa and close proximity to alpine walking trails and Lake Sils.

But with less than a month until her potential run-out in Flushing Meadows, evidence of her practising wearing the boot, on the hotel's clay rather than hard court, might have been cold comfort to those keen to see her back full to fitness.

Raducanu previously shared a video on social media of herself wearing the boot while she practised her serve perched on top of a rubbish bin.

'Not in the bin but on the bin,' she captioned the image with a wink.

Raducanu's withdrawal on the eve of her home Grand Slam saw the player experience a drop in her ranking as she lost the points gained by reaching last year's third round.

In 2025, Raducanu then chased her grass season with a competitive hard-court build-up ahead of New York, reaching the semi-final in Washington, the third round in Montreal, and the second in Cincinnati.

With all those points set to be lost, Raducanu - who is currently ranked 49th in the world - will likely drop out of the top 50 and could possibly lose her standing as British No1 to Katie Boulter, who is currently 20 points behind her compatriot.

Raducanu will also have to prepare for the possibility of a tricky first round at the US Open with no chance of securing a seeded berth.

As she continues to recover from her own injury, she may be watching the travails of her fellow injury-stricken countryman Jack Draper, who was handed a wildcard to play this week's Canada Open in Montreal.

Raducanu described the break at the luxury fitness resort as the 'best reset ever' on Instagram

In a round-up she shared the stunning vistas from the property, which overlooks Lake Sils

Meanwhile with the hard court swing started in earnest, her compatriot Jack Draper is looking to return to competitive action after a similarly injury-stricken 2026

The 24-year-old, who played last year's US Open as the world No5, has seen his early summer injury comeback hampered by continuing issues, forcing his own withdrawal from Wimbledon ahead of the first round and a late withdrawal from last week's Mubadala DC Open in Washington.

Draper, who is coached by tennis legend Andy Murray, has since called for patience and time as he seeks to climb higher than his current No147 ranking.

'It's important for people to recognise that the injury I have is very complex, it's very complicated and everyone around me is doing everything we can to help this keep moving along,' he told Sky Sports on Sunday. 'It's not as simple as "rest and heal up and you'll come back and you'll be fine."

'Everything outside of tennis I'm doing amazingly well, everything on the court I'm managing really well too, so I'm at a point now where I'm happy that I will come through this period.

'It's just going to take some time, but I'm doing all the right things, and the people around me are really supporting me.'

Sports.title: Three Premier League clubs, including a newly-promoted side, enquire over Mykhailo Mudryk after £89m Chelsea winger's doping case is resolved
Sports.content:
Chelsea have received multiple approaches about Mykhailo Mudryk from clubs following the news of his return to football – including three from the Premier League.

Coventry City, managed by Frank Lampard, who worked with Mudryk at Stamford Bridge in 2023, are believed to be among those to have enquired, sources have told Daily Mail Sport.

All options are open between Mudryk and Chelsea this summer, including whether to send him out on loan after his sudden comeback from a doping suspension.

The current plan is for the 25-year-old Ukrainian to be assessed by Xabi Alonso, having travelled to Hong Kong to join his team-mates on their pre-season tour.

Chelsea want to see where their player’s performance levels are now at, with the Ukraine international having not been involved in competitive football since November 2024. That was via his last appearance in a Conference League win away at Heidenheim in which he scored and then disappeared following his failed test.

Another option this summer would be to send Mudryk on loan to Strasbourg, their sister side in France’s Ligue 1. That would allow him to stay under the BlueCo umbrella.

Coventry City, managed by Frank Lampard, who worked with Mudryk at Stamford Bridge in 2023, are believed to be among those to have enquired, sources have told Daily Mail Sport

Wingers are in-demand in this window, which may explain why so many sides are intrigued by Mudryk’s comeback, despite nobody knowing his current fitness levels. His potential was once considered so highly that Chelsea paid £89million to sign him from Shakhtar Donetsk.

Mudryk is effectively a bonus arrival for Chelsea, with Alonso having told reporters after their pre-season loss to Tottenham in Sydney how the news came as a pleasant surprise. He is set to train under Alonso and with the Chelsea squad in Hong Kong, where the club will be facing Juventus in a friendly.

They also have games in Indonesia and Malaysia which will follow, and will be hosting Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge after returning home to London.

If Mudryk was deemed ready to appear in that match, it would represent his first appearance at the Bridge since facing Arsenal in the Premier League there in November 2024. Chelsea beat Mikel Arteta’s club to secure his signature in January 2023.

Mudryk’s return to football was made possible because of a change in the way the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) measures meldonium – the substance for which he tested positive.

WADA increased the threshold by which a player is deemed to have passed the minimum reporting level, from 120 to 150 per cent. In other words, were Mudryk’s sample analysed today, he would not have been deemed to have violated the anti-doping rules.

Mudryk has now managed to come to a resolution with WADA and the Football Association, in which it has essentially been deemed he has served his time for his violation.

He has spent his suspension – described as long and lonely by sources – training almost daily in the hope of returning. That includes renting the pitch at the stadium of non-League side Uxbridge to stage sessions with a private trainer. Chelsea have been highly sympathetic to Mudryk’s situation, having believed his consistent claims of innocence ever since he tested positive.

It was believed to have occurred while he was away with the Ukraine national team in September 2024, and it was after facing Heidenheim in November 2024 that he was informed of his failed test.

Sports.title: England and Wales withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's re-election as FIFA president - days after his plan to sell the World Cup was scuppered
Sports.content:
England and Wales withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's re-election as FIFA president - days after his plan to sell the World Cup was scuppered

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

England will join Wales by withdrawing their letter of support for Gianni Infantino's re-election as FIFA president.

Wales stuck their head above the parapet and became the first nation to explicitly stand against Infantino's re-election as FIFA president on Monday morning.

The Finnish FA have also revoked their support, with more UEFA nations expected to follow after the confederation itself lost confidence.

And now Daily Mail Sport understands the English FA are sending a letter to Infantino, informing the Swiss football administrator that he no longer has their support.

The FA had already articulated their position on Saturday, releasing a statement calling for change at the top of FIFA and declaring a loss of confidence in Infantino.

Withdrawing letters of support is largely symbolic, as associations had already made it clear that Infantino no longer has their support.

However, it does formally reiterate to Infantino that his position is perilous.

The FA had backed Infantino at every opportunity since his initial election in 2016 and were supporting his re-election bid until plans to sell stakes in the World Cup came to light.

His future is now under intense scrutiny after plans to sell a £3.1billion stake in the World Cup to private investors were revealed by The Times.

Those proposals have since been scrapped after opposition from UEFA, the North, Central America and Caribbean confederation (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

But as of July, Infantino had reportedly been endorsed by almost all of FIFA's 211 member associations for re-election. Candidates must be put forward by November 18 and the vote will take place at FIFA's congress in March.

'The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr. Gianni Infantino, for re-election as FIFA President for the 2027–2031 term,' a statement from the Welsh FA reads.

'The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr. Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.'

Wales have become the first nation to withdraw their support for Gianni Infantino's FIFA re-election

Infantino had wanted to sell stakes in the World Cup and FIFA competitions to private investors

He hoped to create a new enterprise with significant investment from Joshua Kushner (pictured) - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law

Infantino has been FIFA president since 2016 after replacing Sepp Blatter and is targeting a fourth term in charge.

But the events of recent days - and the controversies that blighted him before and during the World Cup - have rocked his authority.

His plans have been widely lambasted, including by prime minister Andy Burnham, and two of his closest allies have resigned. Firstly, his senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro stepped down before chief operating officer Kevin Lamour lambasted the proposals.

UEFA and CONCACAF have called on Infantino to quit but their ploy to depose the Swiss football administrator hit a roadblock after Kuwait, Qatar, Sri Lanka and Lebanon reiterated their confidence in his leadership.

UEFA and CONCACAF make up 90 of FIFA's 211 member associations. Although that is above the 20 per cent threshold to trigger a vote of no confidence, it falls short of the majority needed to topple Infantino.

With Infantino retaining support from Africa while South America are expected to take the same position, AFC members would be required to oust the FIFA president.

New Zealand could join Europe and CONCACAF's resistance, but it is doubtful that the remaining 10 members of the Oceania Football Confederation would follow suit.

Infantino wrote to all FIFA nations claiming they would receive £30million if they back his plan to sell off stakes in FIFA's major competitions.

Join the discussion Should football's biggest tournaments ever be open to private investment and ownership?

Carlos Cordeiro (left) quit as an advisor to Gianni Infantino (centre) on Friday

The specific proposal was to sell stakes in the tournament to a group led by Josh Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared. In that light, Infantino's sycophantic behaviour towards Trump - including handing him the inaugural FIFA Peace Price - looks even more suspect.

After his schemes were exposed to the public - very few individuals had known about them - Infantino initially blamed the media for misconstruing them. He has since reneged on his machinations - for now at least.

UEFA welcomed Infantino's abandonment of his plans, writing: 'UEFA welcomes FIFA's decision to withdraw its plan to sell a stake in its competitions - including the World Cup - into private hands.

'The proposal was unanimously rejected by UEFA's national associations and by many other federations and confederations of all sizes around the world, whose job it is to protect football.

'We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

'It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again.

'That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.

'The shabby, back-room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through was anything but transparent. This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.'

FIFA president Infantino pictured with his UEFA counterpart Aleksander Ceferin in 2024; UEFA have strongly opposed Infantino's plot

Countless European nations, including England, Wales, the Netherlands and Norway, endorsed the statement.

A spokeswoman for the English FA added: 'We fully support UEFA's position. It is time for a full and robust review of FIFA's leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart.'

CONCACAF, as they have all week, followed suit: 'CONCACAF and its 41 Member Associations welcome the withdrawal of the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

'The Confederation also commends its 41 Member Associations and the wider football family for the courage and unity they have shown this week.

'At a moment that demanded principled leadership, our members stood together in defence of football's long-term interests and the principles of good governance. That unity has prevailed.

'A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first.

'This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place.

'This concern is not CONCACAF's alone. It is shared across many confederations, Member Associations and those who serve and love the game.

'When people entrusted with protecting the game conclude they can no longer do so from within, the football family is entitled to ask how such a proposal was allowed to proceed, and who bears responsibility for it.'

Infantino has since said: 'The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

'And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

'Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

'Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

'Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, and particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.'

It remains to be seen what happens to the FIFA president, with Infantino having previously been expected to run unopposed in the governing body's elections next March.

That may change now, while FIFA member nations could trigger a vote of no confidence to oust Infantino. The threshold to initiate the process is 46 FIFA member associations. For context, UEFA have 55 members.

Wales have made the first step.

Sports.title: New Arsenal star CHRISTOS TZOLIS hopes to emulate his hero Alexis Sanchez - and reveals how difficult spell at Norwich shaped his career
Sports.content:
New Arsenal star CHRISTOS TZOLIS hopes to emulate his hero Alexis Sanchez - and reveals how difficult spell at Norwich shaped his career

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Christos Tzolis vowed ‘now it’s my time’ after previously struggling in England at Norwich as he looks to emulate his childhood Arsenal idol Alexis Sanchez.

The 24-year-old winger joined the Gunners in a £34million transfer from Club Bruges last month, where he struck an extraordinary 40 goal contributions (17 goals, 23 assists) in 36 league appearances last season.

It’s a steep trajectory from his struggles at Norwich in the Premier League five years ago. He failed to breakthrough, before going on loan spells to FC Twente and Fortuna Dusseldorf — and then making the switch to Belgium.

Though Tzolis feels as though he is now a completely transformed player from the one who last played in the English top-flight.

He said: ‘It was totally different than now. It's always difficult for a team that is promoted from the second division to the Premier League to play high level football.

‘The team I think was not really ready for the Premier League and that makes it also difficult for me to adapt and to play how I could.

Christos Tzolis believes he is a transformed play as he returns to the Premier League with Arsenal

The £34million signing from Club Bruges believes he has similarities to his idol Alexis Sanchez, who starred at Arsenal during four years in North London

‘You can have some setbacks and difficulties. I only learnt a lot of things from this period at Norwich.

‘I have three years in a row that I’m important for my teams and I have a big role in an attacking part. And I feel now more ready to be in the Premier League. Now I have the chance to play for Arsenal. For me, I think I did the right decision after Norwich. I developed myself, I improved a lot. I’m not the same player I was in Norwich, 100 per cent.

‘I feel it also in my body and also in my mindset. Now it’s my time to show that I’m ready and capable of playing in the Premier League.’

He has hit the ground running upon joining Arsenal less than two weeks ago, marking his full debut for the club against Girona on Saturday with a first goal. The winger received the ball on the left before cutting inside and firing his shot into the bottom-right corner via a deflection off Kai Havertz.

Tzolis wears the No17 shirt, which was once donned by his idol Sanchez. He sees similarities between himself and the ex-Gunners forward, who became one of Arsenal’s standout stars during his four years in north London.

‘Actually, I knew that he (Sanchez) was wearing the shirt of number 17,’ said Tzolis. ‘Of course, I watched a lot of football and he was a top player for Arsenal, as a left winger always. He’s one of the players I looked up to when I was younger. And also, I see some similarities with him. But it’s not the reason I took the number 17.

‘It’s nice (though). Alexis Sanchez had number 17 — so I hope I will have the same success.’

He’s certainly already making up for lost time having quickly become the man to beat in fitness tests, according to Ben White.

The England man remarked: ‘Christos has been amazing. He came in, did all the testing, and beat everyone. So he is fitting in really well and everyone is really happy for him to be here.’

Tzolis struggled to make a breakthrough in the Premier League while at Norwich, but has since enjoyed a steep rise leading to champion Arsenal signing him this summer

The Greek winger scored on his first appearance in an Arsenal shirt in their friendly with Girona

Tzolis wholeheartedly agreed. He means business.

‘I know I've won so far,’ he added. ‘There are not all the players here. There are still some players that have to do the tests, of course.

‘But so far I'm first in the fitness test. It's like 20 metres, go back, 40 metres, go back, 60 metres, go back, I think five times in a row. So it's around 1.2k and it's as fast as possible. Actually, it's pretty hard.

‘Actually I had the advantage that I started pre-season also with Bruges so I was already training for two weeks and always I wanted to keep myself fit during summer so I was ready.

‘I came here ready (with) my fitness level and I was happy that I could show it here as well.’

Sports.title: Vinicius Jr to Arsenal transfer hint as key figure flies into London
Sports.content:
Vinicius Jr to Arsenal transfer hint as key figure flies into London

Vinicius Junior might have reported back to Real Madrid for pre-season training, but he is still the subject of growing speculation over a transfer to Arsenal

View 3 Images Vinicius Junior is being eyed for a blockbuster move to Arsenal (Image: (Antonio Villalba/Real Madrid via Getty Images))

Vinicius Jr continues to be linked with a move to Arsenal - and now the president of the agency that represents him has confirmed he is going to be in London. The Gunners have launched a stunning move to sign the Real Madrid star, as Mikel Arteta looks to add some quality to his title-winning squad.

‌



Vinicius, who reported back to Real on Monday for pre-season training, has scored 128 goals in 375 appearances for the La Liga giants, who are keen to keep hold of him this summer. So much so that they have been trying to renew his deal for a number of months now.

‌



The Brazilian's deal expires next summer, and Real opened further talks with him last week in a bid to reach an agreement. But with nothing forthcoming, the La Liga giants have informed the 26-year-old’s camp that the latest contract offer they submitted is final and there will be no further increase or another round of negotiations.

‌



If Vinicius accepts, his deal will be renewed; however, if he rejects the offer, Madrid will open the door to a sale this summer to prevent the Brazilian from entering his final year of contract and leaving for free later, according to Spanish publication Marca.

But now, in an interesting development, the president of Roc Nation Sports confirmed on Monday morning that he is travelling to London. Michael R. Yormark took to Instagram to post an update saying: “London, here I come. Let’s go!”

Arsenal receive immediate response after finally submitting first Bruno Guimaraes offer READ MORE :

Mikel Arteta sends Vinicius Jr transfer message ahead of Real Madrid meeting READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



View 3 Images Michael R. Yormark's post on Instagram

Amid the speculation around the attacker’s Real future, Roc Nation took the unusual step on Sunday by hitting out at 'fake and damaging' reports in a statement shared by Yormark on Instagram. It's not clear whether Roc Nation were speaking about Vinicius and the ongoing rumours surrounding a Real Madrid exit and a move to Arsenal or something else.

But the statement said: "Roc Nation Sports International and our entire team cannot stand idle when unprofessional and uninformed media publish fake and damaging information for attention-seeking purposes.

‌



"This is especially unacceptable when it personally targets our clients without any foundation. It is disruptive, harmful and libellous. Media outlets and journalists need to hold themselves more accountable."

The Gunners have already bolstered their attacking options this summer with the £34million signing of Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge earlier this month. And as well as Vinicius, they're also working on a deal to sign Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United, but have seen their opening offer rejected.

View 3 Images Christos Tzolis in action for Arsenal (Image: Getty Images)

‌



And speaking over the weekend, Gunners boss Arteta admitted: "A lot is happening. We all know about the context of this transfer window.

"From ownership to the board, the sporting director and myself, we know that we want to take this club to a different level. That is going to require a better squad, better individuals.

"We have identified where we have opportunities to grow and to improve and to evolve our game and what is going to be needed to achieve that. Hopefully, very soon we can start to put things in a very concrete way."

Sports.title: Glasgow saved Commonwealth Games - but don't expect them back on UK soil anytime soon
Sports.content:
Glasgow saved Commonwealth Games - but don't expect them back on UK soil anytime soon

Four of the last seven editions have been staged in Great Britain, and it's clear that Commonwealth Sport realises it needs to cut ties to the mother country for its future relevance

View Image The Prince And Princess of Wales attended the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games (Image: Getty)

Glasgow might have saved the Commonwealth Games, but don't expect to see them back on these shores for a generation.

‌



Four of the last seven editions have been staged in Great Britain, and it's clear that Commonwealth Sport realises it needs to cut ties to the mother country for its future relevance. Scotland gets its eternal thanks for stepping in at late notice when Australia said it couldn't afford to host.

‌



Australian taxpayers ended up paying this city £100 million in compensation to stage the Games on their behalf and were duly thanked by topping the medal table with 70 golds.

‌



"Glasgow has acted as a bridge to the future of the Commonwealth Games movement," said Commonwealth Sport president Dr Donald Rukare. "Every host writes its own chapter, and Glasgow's has been one of bravery, courage, friendship and, above all, outstanding innovation."

India will host the centenary Games in 2030, and there are four private expressions of interest for 2034. Nigeria has made no secret of its desire to become the first African host, while New Zealand believes a lower-cost approach to hosting finally gives it a chance to welcome the Commonwealth for the first time since 1990. Canada hasn't hosted since 1994 either.

‌



Insiders admit there is more chance of the Olympics coming back to the UK – with a bid mooted for the 2040s – before another Commonwealth Games. For years, officials presented hosts with a long list of demands and requirements. Glasgow has changed all that.

"It's a much more collaborative process," said Commonwealth Sport chief executive Katie Sadlier. "We're not telling hosts, 'This is what you must do.' Instead, we're asking, 'What are you trying to achieve?' and then working with them to make that happen.

"We've set a guideline of around 15 to 17 sports, but if a future host comes to us with a proposal they believe works for them, we'll sit down and work through it together. We're not imposing rigid targets. We don't want countries building facilities they don't actually need just to host the Games. If a nation genuinely wants to build a stadium because it fits its long-term plans, that's fine, but it shouldn't automatically become part of the Games budget.

Article continues below

"We don't want hosts spending huge amounts of money on things we don't think are necessary any more. Glasgow is using existing venues, stakeholders have accepted reduced service levels, there aren't fleets of VIP cars, and people are travelling by bus. Everyone has embraced that because they wanted the Commonwealth Games to happen."

Sports.title: Emma Finucane roars into history books by completing incredible Commonwealth Games clean sweep
Sports.content:
Emma Finucane roars into history books by completing incredible Commonwealth Games clean sweep

The Welsh wonder crowned a stunning week by adding keirin gold to her time trial, sprint and team sprint titles to cement her status as Britain's undisputed sprint queen

View 2 Images Emma Finucane of Team Wales after her keirin gold at Glasgow 2026 (Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

Four golds. One queen. Emma Finucane roared into the history books by becoming the first sprinter in 96 years to complete a sensational Commonwealth Games clean sweep.

‌



The Welsh wonder crowned a stunning week by adding keirin gold to her time trial, sprint and team sprint titles to cement her status as Britain's undisputed sprint queen. And she barely broke a sweat.

‌



The 23-year-old felt the pressure of becoming the rider everyone wanted to beat after Olympic glory. But in Glasgow, her rivals could only watch her disappear into the distance. She muscled her way to the front with two laps remaining and never looked back, cruising home to claim Wales' 31st medal of the Games.

‌



“I don’t think I’ll ever fully believe I’ve made history here,” the Carmarthen rider said. "It’s surreal. Little me would be absolutely screaming right now. Ten-year-old me would never have imagined this.

“I just hope I’ve inspired people back home to get on a bike or into a velodrome. I’m so glad I found this sport—or maybe it found me. I absolutely love what I do. It feels incredible to have those gold medals. There was definitely a lot of pressure coming in, but I think throughout the week I just focused on riding my own race and letting things unfold naturally.”

The keirin is usually cycling's answer to a pressure cooker – six riders scrapping for every inch behind a pacing bike before the lid blows off in a frantic final lap. But Finucane blew her rivals away long before the final dash. Her decision to hit the front with two laps to go was a huge gamble, handing her rivals the advantage of her slipstream. Yet none could even get close enough to challenge. And this was no easy ride to glory.

‌



While some critics questioned the strength of the Commonwealth Games field, Finucane's rivals included Olympic champion Ellesse Andrews, who took silver while defending her title. Katy Marchant – her Olympic team sprint partner – finished fifth, while fellow Paris gold medallist Sophie Capewell failed to reach the final.

View 2 Images Emma Finucane won a historic four golds at Glasgow 2026 (Photo by Molly Darlington/Getty Images) (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

This was no cakewalk. But Finucane served up another golden masterpiece, insisting she has learned as an athlete since her Paris experience.

‌



“After Paris, everything was a huge learning curve for me emotionally,” she said. "That week was really tough, and what I came away with was hard to process.

“But going into these Games, I’ve learned how to handle pressure better and regulate my emotions more. I definitely felt like I had a target on my back, but I’ve learned to embrace that. I’ve learned how to deal with it better and just focus on improving every day.

“I’m always thinking about the next thing, but I really want to stay in the moment now. That’s something I haven’t always been good at, but I’m trying to change that. Next up, I’m actually going on holiday with my sister. I’ll take a bit of time to reset, then focus on the World Championships. I’ll soak everything in first, because I don’t think it will fully sink in for a while.”

Article continues below

Finucane’s win was the sixth gold medal for Wales on the track and she added she loved singing the anthem.

"I wish I could have stood on the top step in Paris and sung the anthem louder,” she said. "Here, I got to do that, and that means everything to me. I sang every anthem like it was my last. My family being here meant the world."

Sports.title: Josh Kerr outlines next steps after Commonwealth Games glory
Sports.content:
Josh Kerr outlines next steps after Commonwealth Games glory

Kerr has already erased Hicham El Guerrouj's mile world record and the Moroccan's 28-year-old best in the 1500m is next in his sights

View 2 Images Josh Kerr of Scotland with spectators at the Scotstoun Stadium during day nine of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

Josh Kerr knows he's running with a target on his back - and insists he wouldn't have it any other way.

‌



World record holder, Commonwealth champion, it was a whirlwind 24 hours for the new 'King of the Mile'. But Kerr is not the sort to stand still, though he admitted he hadn't had much sleep since his gold medal success at Scotstoun.

‌



"Glasgow on the weekend is always bouncing," he joked.

‌



This was the event he'd had circled in his calendar for some time, but the 28-year-old has new targets in his sights. First, there's regaining the world 1500m title in Beijing next year, then upgrading his Olympic silver from Paris to gold in LA, but top of the list is another world best.

He's already erased Hicham El Guerrouj's mile world record. Perhaps next is the Moroccan's 28-year-old best in the 1500m - the longest-standing running record on the books. Seb Coe, Steve Ovett, and Steve Cram are all former British world record holders in middle-distance running's blue riband event. Kerr makes no secret of the fact he is racing for his legacy too.

In middle-distance running, it's not unknown for in-form athletes to quickly collect records. During a historic 41-day summer stretch in 1979, Coe broke the world records for the 800m, mile and 1500m. Kerr won't compete over 1500m at the European Championships in Birmingham, which perhaps opens up another world record tilt, maybe in Lausanne or Zurich later this summer

‌



“I think the 1,500-world record is within my grasp,” he said. "I'm going to keep going after these records. Unfortunately, I'm the sort of person who gets something and always wants more. We need to keep pushing our sport into the 21st century.

"I don't want to get greedy. Greedy athletes make mistakes, like I did last year at the World Championships. I want to play through all the variables and not push through the red line.

View 2 Images Josh Kerr of Team Scotland celebrates as he crosses the line to win the Men's One Mile Final during the Athletics on day nine of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I'm a body of work built by everyone else around me and I'm incredibly lucky to have the team of people I have supporting me. You don't know how many times you'll get the chance to make history."

Kerr has never hidden his ambitions. He vowed to smash a 27-year-old record and win Commonwealth gold this summer – and no he's delivered on both. Admitting there was relief at backing up his bold talk with action, the Scot insisted he had loved every minute of the pressure.

Sir Chris Hoy, Sir Andy Murray... more of this and it'll surely be "Arise, Sir Josh".

Article continues below

"Chris Hoy went to my school and I was in school assemblies listening to his stories and being inspired," he added. "To be mentioned even in the same sentence as two absolute legends like him and Andy doesn't seem real.

"This job is not easy if you don't have role models and those guys were mine. But I've got a lot of work to do to keep up with them, and I'll try."

Sports.title: Josh Kerr sends clear message after being left hurt by BBC SPOTY snub
Sports.content:
Josh Kerr sends clear message after being left hurt by BBC SPOTY snub

Commonwealth Games and Olympic icon Josh Kerr has opened up on being left out by the BBC

View 2 Images Josh Kerr has opened up on being left off the shortlist (Image: 2026 Ian MacNicol)

Olympic hero Josh Kerr has opened up on his disappointment after being overlooked for the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year award in 2023. The 28-year-old Edinburgh-born star recorded the fastest mile of all time in London two weeks ago and followed it up as he raced to gold at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

‌



The Scot has said he would love to crown his recent achievements by winning the Sports Personality of the Year award. Kerr claimed he was “massively disappointed” to be snubbed from a six-person shortlist for the accolade three years ago after winning the 1500 metres at the World Championships.

‌



The award ultimately went to England goalkeeper Mary Earps. This time, Kerr faces steep competition from England midfielder Jude Bellingham, two-time Masters winner Rory McIlroy, Winter Olympian Matt Weston and darts prodigy Luke Littler.

‌



Speaking about the upcoming December awards, Kerr said: “I'm trying not to build my expectations prematurely for this, though I would absolutely love it. It would be a huge privilege for me, especially since we've seen incredible athletes emerge this year across the Winter Games, the World Cup and all the major rugby tournaments.

“It's tough to stay on par with those incredible competitors, so my plan is simply to stay focused on my own performance, and I just hope people recognise my accomplishments to date.”

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Amy Hunt proud after claiming Commonwealth 100m silver at sodden Scotstoun READ MORE :

The middle-distance runner also hinted at his desire to shatter one more global benchmark before the current campaign concludes.

Just a fortnight ago, he wrote his name into the history books at the London Stadium by completing the mile in 3:42.66. His incredible performance eclipsed the legendary 3:43.13 set by Hicham El Guerrouj in Rome in 1999 by nearly half a second.

Now, Kerr has his sights set on the Moroccan icon’s 1500m record, a milestone that has remained unbroken for an astounding 28 years. El Guerrouj clocked a time of 3:26.00 during a 1998 meet in Rome, and the ambitious Scot is eager to challenge that incredible standard.

‌



“That's clearly our next major target,” he said following his Glasgow victory. “However, I have to be mindful of my physical limits. Ultimately, I'm only human, and the upcoming schedule doesn't offer many opportunities to make a realistic attempt."

View 2 Images Josh Kerr of Team Scotland with a Gold Medal for winning the Mens One Mile Final at Scotstoun Stadium (Image: SNS)

“Because of that, I plan to huddle with my coaches to figure out what is feasible for the remainder of the year. Physically and mentally, I am in a fantastic place.

‌



“I feel fine, though this stretch has definitely been exhausting. Fortunately, I don't have any underlying injuries and remain in peak condition, but I must acknowledge the immense physical demand of the past fortnight. I promise to be completely transparent once we finalise our strategy.”

In addition to his record-breaking ambitions, the runner suggested he is targeting the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, a prestigious invitational event scheduled for Budapest this September.

When questioned about competing in the Hungarian capital, Kerr said: “I think it's entirely possible. We'll be making that choice within the next week or two, and I'll be completely upfront about it. I'll make a public announcement very soon to confirm whether or not I'll be racing.”

Sports.title: Jockey Club quits racecourse body over fears it will continue to 'stifle change'
Sports.content:
Jockey Club quits racecourse body over fears it will continue to 'stifle change'

The Jockey Club announced it will leave the Racecourse Association at the end of 2026, joining Ascot in quitting the trade body amid calls for reform and an independent BHA board

View 2 Images The Jockey Club: which owns Cheltenham is quitting the RCA (Image: PA)

The Jockey Club has confirmed it will depart from the Racecourse Association (RCA) at the end of 2026.

‌



The owner of 15 racecourses, including Cheltenham, Aintree and Newmarket, followed Ascot in declaring it would quit the racecourse body in another setback for the organisation.

‌



On Saturday the RCA unveiled the result of a review, which began in March, under which it would transition away from the one member, one vote framework to a 25 per cent allocation for its four principal groups – Arena Racing Company, the Jockey Club, major independents such as Ascot, York and Newbury and smaller independents.

‌



It would also no longer appoint two members of the BHA board with that responsibility going to representatives independent of the RCA.. However the Jockey Club is unconvinced there is adequate prospect of meaningful reform.

Chief executive Jim Mullen said: "While acknowledging the work that has taken place since March, we have consistently set out throughout the review that it needed to address not just the racecourse voting shares within the RCA, but the organisation's role in representing racecourses politically through its 50% holding of member shares in the BHA.

‌



"This review has addressed the RCA's internal arrangements, but not the constitutional arrangements through which racecourses collectively exercise their influence over the governance of British racing. The RCA's proposals fail to address our fundamental concern that the RCA can continue to act to stifle the necessary changes needed in the industry.

View 2 Images Jim Mullen: Jockey Club CEO (Image: PA)

"Nothing proposed would displace the RCA as the political representative of British racecourses and in our view, confirmed by recent discussions, the RCA would continue to vote against necessary changes such as the introduction of an independent BHA board and substantive changes to the fixture list."

Article continues below

He continued: "It is our intention to work with Ascot Racecourse and other like-minded industry partners to pursue a vision based on the long-term sustainability of the sport and we are in the early stages of establishing a new organisation to do this.

"We accept that other racecourses may wish to pursue different avenues to reform the RCA and we respect their choice, but we believe that at the heart of this debate is the core principle that racing must be able to tackle the challenges it faces, free from self-interest and short-term priorities and this is best achieved by an independent BHA which is able to take input from all stakeholders but ultimately empowered to make timely and effective decisions in the best interests of the sport overall."

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino was set to earn huge salary from World Cup plan as staggering figure revealed
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino was set to earn huge salary from World Cup plan as staggering figure revealed

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino was set to pocket an eye-watering amount should his controversial World Cup idea succeeded

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino has U-turned on the plan to sell a share in the World Cup (Image: Getty Images)

FIFA chief Gianni Infantino was reportedly set to pocket a staggering £47 million per year had his plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup succeeded. Infantino, 56, came under heavy fire after the failed unveiling of his plans to sell off fractions in FIFA competitions to private investors.

‌



The FIFA president's idea plunged the football world into chaos. However, he pulled off a dramatic U-turn after considerable backlash, with pressure now mounting on the Swiss and support for his re-election collapsing.

‌



Infantino's plan was to create a private, investment-open company to run its flagship competitions and raise billions of pounds. It was believed to be led by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, the US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

‌



The FIFA chief, 56, had orchestrated a plan to sell 20 per cent stake in the new sister company to private investors for a reported £3.1m.

UEFA threatened a wide-ranging boycott of any FIFA tournaments, while fellow federations such as CONCACAF and AFC also publicised their opposition to the plan.

English FA follow Wales in withdrawing Gianni Infantino support after botched World Cup plot READ MORE :

FIFA boss Infantino under pressure as UK FA member pulls support READ MORE :

Infantino currently earns a salary of around £2.6m as FIFA president, although his total figure is said to have doubled last year following bonuses. A new role as commissioner of the FIFA Forward Enterprise would, according to The Times, have landed him a salary similar to that of NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, who takes home around £47m per year.

‌



Infantino has been president of FIFA since February 2016, having replaced Sepp Blatter. However, in the wake of his plan falling flat, he is facing unprecedented criticism.

A FIFA statement released last week claimed the idea has been scrapped. Nevertheless, UEFA has declared a loss of confidence in Infantino after the scandal, with the Welsh and English FAs becoming the first nations to publicly withdraw their support for the FIFA boss to be re-elected.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino has been criticised this summer (Image: Getty Images)

‌



UEFA's statement read: "We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

"It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again. That review should be thorough and fundamental.

"No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.

‌



View 3 Images UEFA has 'lost confidence' in Gianni Infantino (Image: Bradley Collyer/PA Wire)

"When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of FIFA's Member Associations to elect him as their President in 2016, he said, 'Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in UEFA. You will have to play a part every day in the life of FIFA,' before telling the assembled stakeholders, 'The money of FIFA is your money. It's not the money of the FIFA President. It's your money. You are the national associations and the money of FIFA has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'

"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent."

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
