See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The coral reef around Bonaire has fallen to about 5% of the seabed, down from more than 60% fifty years ago, researchers told broadcaster NOS on Monday.

The figures come from fieldwork on the Dutch Caribbean island that has not yet been published and which the researchers describe as a first analysis. A Wageningen Marine Research report published last year put average coral cover on Bonaire at under 10% and said algae now dominate the reefs.

The reef is central to a climate case Greenpeace Nederland brought against the Dutch state. Research behind that case found the coral helps shield Bonaire from flooding and that part of the island will be lost as sea levels rise.

The Hague district court ruled in January that Dutch climate policy breached the human rights of Bonaire’s residents and treated them unequally with people in the European Netherlands.

It gave ministers six months to quantify how much greenhouse gas the country can still emit, 18 months to turn that into binding targets, and until 2030 to produce a climate adaptation plan for the island.

The cabinet is appealing but remains bound by the judgment.

Coral researcher Erik Meesters of Wageningen University and Research said warming seawater was the main cause, worsened by a severe El Niño, and that higher temperatures also made coral more prone to disease.

Fast-growing species are surviving, he said, but the large reef-building corals that can reach ten metres are disappearing.

Bonaire’s economy depends heavily on diving tourism. The organisation Reef Renewal said it has planted 20,000 pieces of new coral around the island, while acknowledging the scale is not enough to solve the problem.

World.title: Ferries cancelled as rivers drop to record low levels in drought
World.content:
Several ferries across the Waal and IJssel rivers in Gelderland have been cancelled after the major Dutch rivers dropped to historically low levels in July.

The service across the Pannerdensch Kanaal, near where the Rhine flows into the Waal, between Doornenburg and Pannerden was stopped on Monday morning. The ferry operator said on its website it had taken the decision “to guarantee safety”.

The Rheden ferry, which takes pedestrians and cyclists across the IJssel at Rhederlaag, ran its last service on Monday evening.

Helmsman Richard van Oijen told Omroep Gelderland it was an unprecedented step. “We’ve been out of service in the past, but it was always because of high water.

“This is the first time I can remember not being able to run because of low water.”

Uitwaarde, which runs 10 connecting ferries in Gelderland, has suspended three of its routes across the Waal and Linge rivers because of low water.

The Rhine last week dropped to 6.46m, its lowest level, above sea level at Lobith, the point where the river enters the Netherlands from Germany. This week it is expected to fall another 11 centimetres.

River barges

The flow in the river is down to around one-third of its regular level for July, causing problems for cargo barges and river cruises. Several cruise operators have had to cancel or shorten trips upriver because the water is too low.

Restrictions have also been imposed on river barges, while nearer the river mouth sluice gates have been closed or limited to a few openings a day to prevent sea water getting into the drinking water supply.

The canal locks at Eefde, which up to 20,000 ships pass through a year between the IJssel river and the Twentekanaal, were closed for the first time last Friday, closing off traffic to Almelo, Hengelo and Enschede.

Deventer closed its harbour to shipping for the first time in eight years last week after the IJssel dropped below safe levels.

World.title: Police suspect three explosions in Assen in a week are linked
World.content:
Police have stepped up security outside a house in Assen that has been hit by two explosions in a week.

The third blast was at around midnight on Saturday to Sunday, at the back of the house on Entingestraat, on the northern edge of the Drenthe capital. Nobody was injured.

The first explosion was outside the front of the house in the early hours of Tuesday, two days after another incident the previous weekend in Klaverstraat, on the eastern side of the town.

Police have placed cameras on poles outside both addresses and are investigating if the explosions are linked. They have appealed for witnesses or anyone with camera footage from the area to contact them on the non-emergency number 0900 8844.

World.title: Police arrest two after Amsterdam war memorial defaced
World.content:
Two men have been arrested after the national war memorial on the Dam in central Amsterdam was defaced early on Sunday morning.

Texts were sprayed on the monument in yellow and blue paint at around 5.15am, including a skull. Police said they have not yet established a motive.

A 27-year-old man from Hoofddorp was detained after a patrol car happened to pass through the square while he was using a spray can, a police spokesperson said. A 39-year-old Polish man was caught shortly afterwards writing on the back of the monument in lipstick.

Police could not say whether the two knew each other. The monument was cordoned off with tape while cleaners removed the paint.

Mayor Femke Halsema wrote on social media that it was appalling that the monument had been targeted again, and praised officers for making immediate arrests.

The memorial, unveiled in 1956, commemorates the Dutch war dead and is the site of the annual Remembrance Day ceremony on May 4. It was sprayed with red paint hours before this year’s ceremony, and daubed during a pro-Palestinian demonstration in 2025.

A court found the man responsible for the 2025 incident guilty last month but imposed no punishment, ruling that defacing the memorial was socially unacceptable and disproportionate whatever the political message behind it.

Train services between The Hague and Delft were suspended on Monday after a dog ran onto the track.

The disruptions began at 8am when a train had to stop to avoid hitting the animal. All main line services have been cancelled until at least 10.30am, including Intercity trains from Hollands Spoor station to Breda and Sprinter trains between The Hague and Dordrecht.

Trams between The Hague and Delft are running as normal. Passengers are advised to check the NS travel planner before setting out.

The setback happened just as services between The Hague and Utrecht resumed following work to repair a broken overhead power line.

NS said the cable was damaged by a train passing through Gouda on Sunday afternoon. The stranded train had to be led away before the power lines could be fixed. Replacement buses were laid on to transport passengers between Gouda and Lansingerland-Zoetermeer.

Polish swimmer Bartłomiej Kubkowski has become the first person in history to swim across the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Poland, covering a distance of just over 160 kilometres (99 miles). On Sunday evening, an exhausted Kubkowski clambered onto the beach in the town of Dziwnów on Poland’s northern Baltic coast, around 56 hours after he had set off from Kaseberga in Sweden on Friday. The achievement marks a personal triumph for Kubkowski, for whom this was the fifth attempt to complete the route. His effort this year has raised over 715,000 zloty (€166,000) for children’s cancer treatment so far, with donations to his fundraiser still coming in. View this post on Instagram A post shared by PURELY ATHLETICS (@purelyathletics) During the crossing, Kubkowski was unable to sleep and, although a support boat accompanied him and provided food and drink, he was not allowed to touch the vessel itself. His journey of around 160km was not far off the longest-ever continuous, unassisted open-water swim ratified by the Marathon Swimmers Federation, which was the 168.3 km swum by American Sarah Thomas in 2017 in Lake Champlain, between the US states of New York and Vermont. Kubkowski has been attempting to swim the route between Sweden and Poland since 2022, getting progressively closer to achieving the goal. Last year, he came within 11km of the Polish coast before extreme exhaustion and deteriorating weather forced him to give up, reported Eurosport. However, Kubkowski, a former competitive swimmer who now devotes himself to ultraswimming, did last year manage to break the world record for the longest distance swum in a swimming pool over 24 hours, after he managed to cover 103.6 km (64.5 miles). Another Polish swimmer, Karolina Szczepaniak, is also currently attempting to swim from Sweden to Poland along a slightly different route to Kubkowski’s. At the time of writing, she is around 110km into the 172km journey, and has raised almost 400,000 zloty for charity. Szczepaniak, a former Olympic swimmer, also attempted the feat last year, but was forced to give up after 57 hours amid worsening weather. However, the 146.7km she swam set a new record for the longest distance covered by a female swimmer in the Baltic Sea and a Polish record for open-water swimming by a woman. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. World.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and preschools in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and preschools will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to preschools. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. The missile entered Poland during a period of intensive overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, travelling around 100 km over Polish territory before exploding in a field in the Lublin region on Thursday morning. Nie miejmy żadnych złudzeń. Tego typu sytuacje albo tego typu prowokacje będą się zdarzać – powiedział wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk w @faktypofaktach, komentując wybuch rakiety na Lubelszczyźnie.https://t.co/IKxuGNwe05 — tvn24 (@tvn24) July 30, 2026 “We can confidently confirm that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile, a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact,” deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk told broadcaster TVN24 late on Thursday. The object was “a potentially very dangerous missile,” Tomczyk added. Asked whether the incident could have been a deliberate move by Moscow, he said that no possibilities could be ruled out. “We don’t know, and if we do find out, it will mainly be through intelligence. I’m sure the coming weeks will provide us with more answers,” the deputy minister said. Tomczyk said Poland was working closely with Ukraine, adding that 20 of the roughly 70 missiles fired by Russia overnight from Wednesday to Thursday were at one point heading towards Poland. “It is also worth noting that the vast majority of these missiles were shot down by Ukraine over Ukrainian territory, which clearly bore the full brunt of the attack,” he said. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. An object crashed into a field 100 km from Poland’s border with Ukraine overnight after a major Russian attack. Investigators collected fragments and soil samples from the impact site, where the explosion left a crater around 10 metres wide and 5 metres deep. “The crater has been filled and the site handed back to its owner. The Territorial Defence Force combed through an area of approximately 3 km² and found numerous rocket debris, including propulsion components,” the Lublin prosecutor’s office said. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Kolumbii 🇨🇴, który na terenie Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau propagował nazizm i znieważył miejsce pamięci. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. In her new position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. World.title: Martini Opens Its First Central European Terrazza in Prague
World.content:
Prague has become home to the first Martini Terrazza in Central Europe, with the Italian drinks brand opening a new rooftop venue at the Máj Národní department store.

The summer terrace is located on the Fly Vista rooftop, offering cocktails, food and views across the Prague skyline. The concept is designed around the Italian aperitivo tradition and is intended as a seasonal meeting place during the summer months.

Martini Terrazza venues have previously appeared in other European cities and holiday destinations. The Prague location brings the same format to the Czech capital, combining the brand’s drinks with music, themed evenings and social events.



The drinks menu includes several Martini-based cocktails, including Martini Bianco Spritz, Martini Fiero & Tonic and the Americano. Visitors can also order non-alcoholic Martini Spritz options, alongside a selection of food designed to accompany the drinks.

The terrace is scheduled to remain open throughout the summer season.

Martini has been associated with the Italian aperitivo tradition for more than 160 years. In the Czech Republic, the brand is distributed by Coca-Cola HBC Czech Republic and Slovakia.

“Prague has become the home of the first Martini Terrazza in Central Europe,” said Kateřina Valoušková, Martini Brand Manager at Coca-Cola HBC Czech Republic and Slovakia. She said the concept reflects Martini’s long-standing connection with the Italian aperitivo and social occasions.

World.title: World-Famous DJ Tiësto Returns to Prague on August 23
World.content:
Dutch DJ and producer Tiësto is returning to Prague on August 23, with a performance scheduled at DupleX Prague.

One of the most recognizable names in electronic music, Tiësto has been a major figure in the international dance scene for more than two decades. His Prague appearance will bring him back to the city for another night at the popular rooftop club in the centre of Prague.

The event is expected to feature a mix of Tiësto’s well-known tracks and newer material, alongside the production and atmosphere that have become a regular part of his live shows.

Tiësto, whose real name is Tijs Verwest, began his career in the Dutch club scene before becoming internationally known through his work in trance music.



Over the years, his sound has developed considerably, moving towards house, EDM and more mainstream dance music.

He has since performed at some of the world’s largest festivals and venues and worked with a wide range of artists. His music has also reached audiences well beyond the traditional electronic music scene, helping establish him as one of the genre’s most commercially successful artists.

Tickets are on sale through the official DupleX website.

New album

Tiësto is working on a new album that will see him return to his trance roots.

The Dutch DJ said he had recently “got re-inspired by trance music” and was gradually bringing the genre back into his sound. He said he hopes to finish the album soon.

The project follows “Bring Me To Life,” released last November as the first taste of what Tiësto said his 2026 album could sound like.

World.title: Spaniard Santi Denia Named Coach of the Czech Republic National Team
World.content:
Spanish coach Santi Denia took over the Czech Republic national team on Friday to become the first foreigner in the post.

The Czech soccer association said the 52-year-old signed a two-year contract with an option to be extended by another two years.

Czech football association head David Trunda introduced Denia at a news conference in Prague.

“We greatly appreciate that an expert with such a credit and immense experience at the international level is joining the Czech national team,” Trunda said.



“I’m happy to be here and I’m extremely motivated, because I consider it a great opportunity to lead the Czech national team,” Denia said. “Czech football has a magnificent history and I honestly regard it as a great honor to be here.”

Denia replaced Miroslav Koubek who resigned after the team’s early exit from the World Cup.

Denia was a center-back in Atletico Madrid (1994-2005) and has two games on the national team to his credit.

As coach, he led Spain to gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He also claimed the European titles with Spain´s under-17 (2017) and under-19 teams (2019).

He was most recently in charge of Al-Shahania, a club in Qatar.

His first major task in the post will be to face tough opponents in League A of the Nations League. The Czechs open the competition by hosting Croatia on Sept. 26 in a group which also includes England and World Cup champions Spain.

World.title: Czech PM Calls for Closing Schengen to Spain due to Migration Crisis in Ceuta
World.content:
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for temporarily excluding Spain from Schengen due to the migration crisis in Ceuta, where about 49,000 migrants entered uncontrollably from Morocco.

Italy has already suspended Schengen rules in connection with Spain.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for closing the Schengen zone to Spain after a sharp escalation of the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

According to Babiš, the situation in Ceuta is “absolutely scandalous,” and the cause of the crisis was the overly lenient migration policy of the Spanish authorities.



According to the publication, since Thursday, about 49,000 migrants have entered Ceuta uncontrollably from the territory of Morocco. At least 19 people have died trying to cross the maritime border.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) described the situation as a serious challenge for the entire Schengen Area but stopped short of calling for Spain’s exclusion, saying he wanted to hear Madrid’s position before drawing conclusions.

What is the Schengen Agreement?

The Schengen Area allows people to travel between 29 European countries without routine passport checks at internal borders.

While border controls are normally abolished, member states can temporarily reinstate them if they believe there is a serious threat to public order or internal security.

Italy does not share a land border with Spain, so the decision to reintroduce border controls for a month will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries.

Where is Ceuta?

Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa that borders Morocco.

Spain also controls the nearby city of Melilla. Together, the two enclaves form the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

Roughly the size of inner Sydney, Ceuta has a population of just over 83,000, according to Spain’s Instituto Nacional de Estadistica. It is home to Christian and Muslim communities, including Spanish and Moroccan residents and cross-border workers.

World.title: Prague’s Online Heat Map Shows Where to Find Water and Shade
World.content:
As another spell of extreme summer heat approaches the Czech Republic, Prague has published an online map showing where residents can cool down, find drinking water or spend time near water.

Temperatures in the capital could reach 38°C, with the hottest conditions expected toward the end of the week.

This map is designed to help people find relief across the city and includes public drinking fountains, misting systems, fountains, wells and locations suitable for swimming or relaxing beside the water.

The project was prepared by the City of Prague in cooperation with the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR Prague) and the municipal technology company Operátor ICT.



The initiative is part of the city’s broader efforts to prepare for more frequent periods of extreme heat. Prague says it is increasingly focusing on measures that can reduce the effects of rising temperatures over the longer term, rather than relying only on temporary interventions.

More trees, water and shade planned

Prague is also looking to incorporate more greenery and water into public spaces as part of new development projects.

The city is supporting measures including new fountains and other water features, green roofs, rainwater collection tanks, climbing plants, permeable surfaces and additional tree planting. The expansion of parks is also among the measures being considered.

Temperatures could approach 40°C

The current heatwave is expected to reach its peak on Friday, when temperatures could climb as high as 39°C in parts of the Czech Republic.

Friday night could also remain exceptionally warm, with overnight temperatures staying above 20°C in some areas.

A temporary change is expected on Saturday, particularly in parts of the country where showers and thunderstorms could bring some relief. The cooler conditions, however, are not expected to last.

At the beginning of next week, temperatures are forecast to rise again, with daytime highs between 32°C and 37°C.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum.

It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: Prague Pride Strengthens Security Measures Following Berlin Attack
World.content:
Security will be tightened at this year’s Prague Pride festival following a deadly attack at a similar event in Berlin.

Czech police are preparing additional measures to protect participants in the week-long festival, which begins Monday.

The measures will also reflect changes to this year’s festival route and venue.

Prague Pride is moving its main festival area from Letná Plain to Štvanice Island. The traditional Saturday parade will also follow a new route, starting in the lower section of Wenceslas Square, continuing through the historic center and ending at Štvanice.



Organizers will begin the parade with a minute of silence on Wenceslas Square to remember the person killed in the Berlin attack.

“Thousands of people standing in silence will be a reminder that we will definitely not remain silent about violence motivated by prejudice,” Prague Pride director Kamila Fröhlichová said.

This year’s Prague Pride will feature more than 100 cultural, educational and social events. Dozens of associations, institutions, companies and individuals will organize programs at venues across the capital.

While many events will focus on the lives and experiences of LGBTQ+ people, the festival will also address wider questions surrounding human rights and civil society. A full program is available on the Prague Pride website.

Prague Pride was first held in August 2011. Its inaugural edition was met with strong opposition from conservative groups and politicians, who described the parade as obscene and accused its organizers of promoting what they called an “ideology of homosexuality.”

Then-President Václav Klaus was among the most prominent critics, arguing that society needed to oppose what he described as the spread of homosexuality.

Protests continued in subsequent years but gradually declined in size and intensity.

World.title: Prague Opens Air-Conditioned Space in City Centre to Help Beat Heat Wave
World.content:
People looking for relief from the heat in central Prague can use the air-conditioned ground floor of the Škoda Palace in Jungmannova Street on Thursday and Friday.

The city has opened the space to the public as temperatures across the Czech Republic are expected to rise well above 30°C. The building will be accessible from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on both days.

Visitors can sit on benches and chairs, refill their water bottles at drinking fountains and use the toilets. Drinks and snacks are also available for purchase.



The measure comes as the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute has warned of very high temperatures in parts of the country. Forecasters are advising people to drink regularly, stay out of direct sunlight where possible and avoid strenuous physical activity, particularly during the afternoon.

The Czech Republic is facing several days of intense heat, with Friday expected to be among the hottest day of the current spell. Temperatures above 35°C are possible in some areas.

Individual Prague districts are taking similar steps. Prague 3, for example, plans to make air-conditioned areas in its town hall, information centre and Žižkostel available to the public when temperatures are forecast to exceed 35°C. Visitors will be able to sit down, drink water and take a break from the heat.

The city says the cooling spaces are intended to provide temporary relief during the hottest periods, particularly for people who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.

World.title: Underage Ukrainian boy threatened to blow up Hungarian and Russian schools
World.content:
The Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office has brought charges against a Ukrainian boy and is seeking a custodial sentence to be served in a juvenile detention facility over bomb threats sent to mostly Budapest schools last spring, the prosecution said on Monday.

Minor Ukrainian boy threatened to blow up schools in Hungary

According to the statement, the 17-year-old arrived in Hungary with his family in 2022 and was granted asylum in the summer of 2024; he continued his studies at a school in Budapest.

In March 2025, the minor began promoting what he called an extremist “new-generation plan”, with the aim of intimidating pupils and teachers in his circle, as well as followers on his social media accounts, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

As part of that campaign, between 12 March and 30 April 2025, he sent threatening messages from his mobile phone to the official email addresses of eight Budapest educational institutions — including his own — and one school in Russia, while using computer methods designed to prevent the sender from being identified.

If you missed – Putin again suggests Hungary could regain territory from Ukraine: what he may have meant

Nine acts of terrorism

In those messages, he claimed on behalf of a multi-person organisation that bombs had been placed in the school buildings and warned that, unless they were evacuated, they would be blown up.

The authorities evacuated the threatened schools after every message. Pupils and teachers were only allowed back in after explosive ordnance checks, and the cost of evacuations and searches came to roughly 300,000 forints, the statement said.

The Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office has charged the juvenile defendant with threatening to commit nine acts of terrorism and is seeking a prison sentence to be served in a juvenile detention facility.

He had previously been remanded in custody and is currently under criminal supervision, the statement added.

Hungarian lawyers’ circle head: former PM Orbán may soon become a suspect – can he be arrested?

World.title: The full damage is only visible at record-low water levels – why is the Danube still being polluted? – photos
World.content:
A yellow-green, foul-smelling liquid is continuing to seep into the Danube at Óbuda every time water levels fall to unusually low levels — yet nothing is being done. The state-owned company responsible has so far produced plans and more plans, while a fraction of its profits would be enough to clean up the site and hand Budapest a major brownfield development opportunity. So what is happening at the Óbuda Gas Works?

Everyone knows about it, but nothing happens in practice

For decades, a severe environmental legacy has lain beneath one of the most valuable stretches of the Danube embankment in Budapest. During more than 70 years of operation, between 1913 and 1984, around 200,000 tonnes of hazardous, carcinogenic material were buried in the soil of the former Óbuda Gas Works. As that contamination leaches into the groundwater, it continues to pollute the Óbuda stretch of the Danube whenever water levels are low.

As a result of the gas works’ coal coking and coal-tar processing operations, the soil was heavily contaminated with naphthalenes, toxic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), xylenes, carcinogenic benzene and arsenic. At the time, it appears nobody thought this might become a problem — yet the environmental damage has been well known since at least 1990.

Why is the pollution reaching the Danube?

The contaminated groundwater flows towards the Óbuda branch of the Danube. When water levels are high, the river’s pressure partly holds back this movement. But when levels drop, the counter-pressure weakens and the polluted groundwater can reach the river. Previous studies have documented the phenomenon, but with water levels now exceptionally low, it is also plainly visible to the naked eye: a yellow-green, highly toxic, foul-smelling substance is seeping almost continuously into the river. The cut-off wall only partly contains it.

Who must pay for the clean-up?

Under the “polluter pays” principle, the remediation is the responsibility of the successor to the former municipal utility FŐGÁZ. After FŐGÁZ was transferred into state ownership, that obligation ultimately passed to the state and is now tied to the state-owned MVM Next Zrt. Graphisoft Park bought the southern part of the site in 1996 on the basis that, under the purchase agreement, clean-up remained the seller’s responsibility. Yet work has still not begun.

In 2015, when remediation was still the responsibility of the then municipal FŐGÁZ, the authorities approved a detailed intervention plan under which the clean-up should have been completed by 2017, or by 2019 at the latest. But later procurement procedures revealed that the previously ring-fenced 6.6 billion forints, plus an additional 1.5 billion from each of FŐGÁZ’s then owners, RWE and the city of Budapest, would not be enough: the estimate had already risen to around 20 billion forints.

A Danube beach in Budapest. Photo: Facebook/Karácsony Gergely

The original solution was to dig out the contaminated soil, transport it away and dump it elsewhere. But there were serious logistical obstacles: there was not enough landfill capacity in Hungary, and the work would have meant as many as 50 to 60 lorry loads of hazardous waste a day. An in-situ physical and chemical treatment was also examined, but no acceptable solution was found.

Another deadline, another procedure, another delay

The deadlines previously set have been changed several times. Under the current timetable, the earlier intervention and monitoring plan should be reviewed by 31 December 2026. Graphisoft Park challenged this, and the Budapest municipal council joined the legal action, arguing that the arbitrary alteration of deadlines by the previous government was unacceptable. A court struck down the decision in 2025, meaning the 31 December 2026 date is not currently a valid remediation deadline.

Historic drought. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

Is there money for the clean-up?

Costs have risen sharply over the years. Alongside the earlier estimate of about 20 billion forints, there were already reports in 2025 that a complete soil replacement could cost 30 to 40 billion forints. However, the multi-billion environmental reserve set aside at MVM relates to several inherited contamination sites, so it does not follow that such sums are available specifically for the Óbuda Gas Works. A proposal submitted in December 2024 by the Podmaniczky Movement, then led by Dávid Vitézy, now transport minister, argued that MVM’s profits alone would be enough to carry out the work from only a small part of them.

MVM, however, says a new technology must be found that can deliver the work more efficiently and with a lower environmental burden than before. The problem is that further studies, permits and legal procedures only delay any real intervention.

Water and energy crisis: even one of Orbán’s former strongmen admits their failure

Is Budapest’s tap water safe?

Yes. Budapest’s tap water is currently safe and drinkable, and the municipal water utility regularly checks water quality to ensure it meets the required standards. That does not mean, however, that the gas works contamination poses no environmental risk. A significant share of Budapest’s drinking water supply is based on bank-filtered water sources, which makes protecting the Danube’s water quality a long-term priority.

The Óbuda Gas Works pollution therefore does not currently make Budapest’s tap water unsafe, but the discharge of hazardous substances into the river is a problem that should be eliminated through remediation.

The contamination has been known about since the early 1990s. Since then, there have been plans, deadlines, technical studies and legal proceedings — yet actual remediation has still not begun. The question now is no longer whether the problem exists, but when the toxic material will finally start to be removed from the Óbuda Gas Works site.

World.title: Breaking – Botond Feledy to lead the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs
World.content:
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has selected foreign policy expert Botond Feledy to lead the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, Hungary’s state-backed foreign policy research institute. Feledy accepted the position, saying his two decades of professional experience had prepared him for the role.

Anita Orbán: central role in the professional preparation

The appointment was announced on Monday, 3 August. The Hungarian Institute of International Affairs – which is Magyar Külügyi Intézet in Hungarian – will also return from the Prime Minister’s Office to the supervision of the Foreign Ministry.

In a statement announcing the decision, Orbán said the institute would once again play a central role in the professional preparation of Hungarian foreign policy decisions. Hungarian Institute of International Affairs to receive renewed strategic role

According to the foreign minister, the institution’s work will focus on providing decision-makers with independent, forward-looking research, analysis and forecasts.

Orbán said international summits and high-level diplomatic negotiations were only the visible elements of foreign policy. Behind them, she added, extensive preparatory work was required to identify Hungary’s national interests, understand major shifts in global politics and assess how international developments could affect the country’s security, economy and room for manoeuvre.

Hungarian Institute of International Affairs: strategic and analytical thinking

The Hungarian Institute of International Affairs is therefore expected to strengthen strategic and analytical thinking within Hungary’s foreign policy apparatus. The ministry also wants the organisation to contribute to public discussion about international affairs rather than operate solely as a closed government research centre.

Feledy expressed a similar ambition in a Facebook post confirming that he had accepted the minister’s invitation.

“If the homeland calls, one cannot say no – this is the first time I have truly understood what that sentence means,” he wrote. Feledy described the role as both a major opportunity and an honour, noting that the institute’s researchers would support Hungary’s entire foreign affairs apparatus. He added that its responsibilities would range from training a new generation of experts to making foreign policy more accessible to society.

“We will certainly not be building only an ivory tower,” he wrote.

Who is Botond Feledy?

Feledy has worked in foreign policy journalism, analysis, education and talent development for approximately 20 years. He studied at Sciences Po Bordeaux, Paris-Panthéon-Assas University, the Free University of Berlin and Budapest’s Eötvös Loránd University. His professional work has focused primarily on Euro-Atlantic security policy, information warfare and cybersecurity.

He previously headed the Brussels-based European Leadership Programme and served as managing director of Red Snow Consulting. He has taught international relations at Eötvös Loránd University and Pázmány Péter Catholic University in Budapest, as well as at Sciences Po’s campus in Dijon.

Until 2017, Feledy served as director of the Saint Ignatius Jesuit College of Advanced Studies in Budapest. He has also been involved in several Hungarian organisations and initiatives working in higher education and talent development.

In 2007, he co-founded Kitekinto.hu, one of Hungary’s first news sites dedicated specifically to international and foreign policy affairs. Between 2011 and 2012, he headed the foreign affairs desk of Hungary’s state news agency, MTI. More recently, he worked as a foreign policy commentator, podcast host and author of the HetiFeledy international affairs newsletter published by Partizán for four years.

Cyberattack hits Hungary’s State Treasury as experts trace attack to Russian servers

Gladden Pappin leaves institute

Feledy succeeds American political theorist Gladden Pappin, whose resignation was accepted by Orbán on Friday, 31 July. The foreign minister thanked Pappin for his committed work and his efforts to support the development of the institute. Pappin had led the organisation while it operated under the Prime Minister’s Office.

The leadership change coincides with a wider institutional reorganisation following the formation of the Tisza government. Under the new structure, the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs will again operate under the Foreign Ministry, with its principal task being to provide research-based support for foreign policy decisions.

Feledy’s appointment signals an effort to combine government-oriented strategic analysis with education and broader public engagement. The next major indication of the institute’s direction will be its future research programme and the extent to which its work becomes visible in Hungary’s foreign policy decision-making.

Hungary recalls 25 more ambassadors, including from Washington, London, Brussels, Moscow and Kyiv

World.title: Water and energy crisis: even one of Orbán’s former strongmen admits their failure – updated
World.content:
For years, the distribution of rainfall across the Carpathian Basin has become ever more extreme. Experts have long warned that there is no sign of any reversal in the trend, and that the climate crisis will only deepen the drying-out of the region. Yet the previous government did nothing to address the problem. That is now being acknowledged not by just anyone, but by one of Orbán’s most powerful former ministers — in total contradiction of the communication line now being pushed by Fidesz, which has gone into opposition. In part, then, he has admitted that the previous government, in which he served as minister for construction and transport, bears responsibility for today’s water and energy crisis by failing to act.

Warnings over water and energy crisis for years

Researchers warned years ago that the intensity and frequency of extreme rainfall events were increasing. In other words, the total amount of precipitation does not necessarily fall, but its distribution can become drastically more uneven, creating major challenges across everything from Hungarian agriculture to many aspects of everyday life.

The Carpathian Basin has, roughly since the 19th century, been re-engineered through drainage and other measures to get rid of incoming water as quickly as possible, so that the once widespread areas of inland flooding could disappear and be replaced by land suitable for arable farming. But as rainfall becomes ever more erratic, life-giving water now leaves the basin too quickly, leaving behind dry, increasingly desert-like terrain. We wrote separately last year about a future Hungarian desert that could affect the lives of several hundred thousand people.

Is this the future Hungarian landscape? Source: depositphotos.com

Blunt words from a former minister

The previous Orbán governments could have done far more to improve the situation, and perhaps Hungary would not now — in the midst of this year’s second heat dome and a prolonged, historic drought — be on the brink of yet another energy crisis. Opposition MPs, as well as government-aligned Tisza politicians and ministers, have repeatedly condemned previous governments over this, but Telex has found the parliamentary record in which even one of the fifth Orbán government’s most powerful men, János Lázár, acknowledged grave failures and shortcomings. In December last year, before the Committee on Sustainable Development, he said things such as:

“The government made a mistake when it did not build large reservoirs ten years ago.”

“You are absolutely right in saying that it is madness for us to let out far more fresh water than comes into the country. It is an unsustainable situation.”

“Let me share with you a government secret: this is discussed extremely often within government circles. […] Today, 200 millimetres of water are missing from the land on the Great Plain.”

“Your figures are entirely correct. Water shortage means a brutal reality, and I can only say that there is no real decision on what we actually want.”

Lázár János won a seat at the April election as well, but despite being one of the faces of the Fidesz campaign, he is among the least frequent attendees in the Hungarian parliament, and his political communication has been effectively non-existent since the Orbán government’s defeat.

Good news from PM Péter Magyar: Paks NPP may operate longer than thought

Hungary faces water and energy crisis

The Paks Nuclear Power Plant is expected to shut down completely today because there is not enough water in the Danube. No barrage is operating on Hungary’s stretch of the river, so there is no reserve from which to draw; the only water available is what flows through the country. At present, that is far too little. Water level yesterday afternoon stood at minus 133 centimetres, a historic low.

The gradual shutdown of the Paks NPP. Photo: Facebook/MVM Paksi Atomerőmű Zrt.

Forecasts suggest that the heat dome will remain in place for at least another four to five days, and there is no immediate end in sight to the historic drought either, so the level will continue to fall. Within days or weeks, for example, the popular Lake Velence — the familiar, continuous sheet of water used for festivals, sport and tourism — may cease to exist as we know it.

Update: Forsthoffer urges cooperation among political actors

The situation caused by the drought and the heatwave is grave, and it transcends politics, Forsthoffer, the speaker of parliament exercising the rights of the president of the republic, said on Monday, calling on political actors to work together for a common responsibility.

Speaking at a press conference after a meeting with the prime minister and the leaders of parliamentary party groups at the presidential Sándor Palace, Forsthoffer said she had not called the meeting to ask anyone to “abandon their ideological principles”.

Forsthoffer said the drought and heatwave affected both government and opposition voters, adding that she wanted to discuss with the attendees how they could collectively project calm, demonstrate cooperation and support mutually agreeable measures.

She said she had asked Prime Minister Peter Magyar to brief the group leaders on the measures taken by the government. She noted that since this week’s special session of parliament was cancelled, she wanted to ensure that the party leaders could address their questions directly to the prime minister.

World.title: Good news from PM Péter Magyar: Paks NPP may operate longer than thought
World.content:
Cooling water volume could be sufficient to keep the last turbine operating at the Paks nuclear power plant through Monday or even Tuesday, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in a video message posted on Facebook.

Péter Magyar: Paks NPP may operate for days

Keeping the block — generating 240 MW at present — online is “very good news”, Péter Magyar said. He added that voluntary measures by industrial, institutional and household consumers had reduced electricity consumption by 700 MW on Sunday.

Output of the Paks NPP has gradually been scaled back over the past week as water levels on the Danube — used to cool the plant — reached record lows.

He added that, because water levels are expected to fall further, the possibility of shutting down the Paks nuclear power plant remains on the table, but everyone is working to ensure the last turbine can keep operating for as long as possible, under the highest standards of safety.

Source: Paks Nuclear Power Plant / Facebook

“The full guarantee of nuclear safety is a basic expectation from which no one can deviate; that will always remain the top priority,” the prime minister stressed.

If you missed: Budapest shuts down 40 fountains as emergency water-saving measures begin

Péter Magyar said that on Sunday Hungarians — households, businesses, local councils and institutions alike — saved 700 megawatts of electricity, equivalent to the output of one and a half Paks reactor blocks, together.

Interim President Ágnes Forsthoffer calls government and parliamentary party leaders to talks

Agnes Forsthoffer has asked the prime minister for an urgent, off-schedule briefing on the situation caused by the exceptional heatwave, and on the government’s response to it, the Sándor Palace said on Sunday, according to MTI. She has also invited the parliamentary parties’ group leaders to Monday’s meeting. Both the prime minister and the group leaders have accepted the invitation.

World.title: Cyberattack hits Hungary’s State Treasury as experts trace attack to Russian servers
World.content:
Hungary’s State Treasury has confirmed that part of its IT infrastructure was hit by a cyberattack, with preliminary findings indicating that the attack originated from Russian servers.

According to the Treasury, the incident targeted the IT network of its Agriculture and Rural Development Division, which operates as Hungary’s National Paying Agency responsible for administering agricultural and rural development funds.

Infected servers isolated immediately

The Treasury told Telex that its IT specialists acted as soon as the attack was detected, disconnecting the affected servers from the network to prevent further damage.

Officials stressed that no customer data has been compromised and that there is currently no evidence of data loss.

However, the attack did affect some internal systems. Files stored on the computers of certain employees became encrypted, suggesting that the attackers deployed ransomware or similar malicious software.

Investigation under way

The incident is being investigated with the assistance of experts from Hungary’s National Cyber Security Centre, who are working alongside Treasury specialists to contain the attack and restore secure operations as quickly as possible.

The Treasury has also notified Hungary’s National Authority for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (NAIH), as required under applicable regulations. According to Hungarian media reports, the case is also being examined by the National Bureau of Investigation and the Special Service for National Security.

If you missed it: Hungarian foreign ministry was aware of Russian cyber attacks, insider documents prove

Some online services temporarily unavailable

While the investigation continues, certain electronic services used by the Agriculture and Rural Development Division will remain available only on a limited basis for security reasons. The Treasury apologised for any inconvenience caused by temporary service disruptions and asked users for their patience while recovery efforts continue.

Although experts currently believe the attack originated from Russian servers, authorities have not publicly identified the individuals or group responsible, and the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Budapest shuts down 40 fountains as emergency water-saving measures begin
World.content:
Budapest has switched off 40 public fountains and artificial waterfalls as authorities step up emergency measures to conserve water during Hungary’s worsening drought and heatwave.

The announcement was made by Péter Dezsényi, managing director of the city’s park maintenance company FŐKERT, who said an emergency climate response plan is now being prepared following the introduction of extraordinary water restrictions.

Water use must be cut without sacrificing Budapest’s green heritage

According to Dezsényi, many municipalities and private garden owners have been asking whether they should stop watering altogether. His answer is clear: reduce water consumption dramatically, but do so strategically.

He warned that Budapest’s parks, trees and gardens represent an estimated HUF 400 billion (around EUR 1.1 billion) in living natural assets built up over the past 100 to 150 years. Allowing them to die would take years (or even decades) to reverse.

“In a normal hot August, watering parks and gardens can account for up to 10% of the city’s total drinking water consumption,” he explained. “That must now be significantly reduced, while causing as little ecological damage as possible.”

Young trees come first, lawns can wait

FŐKERT outlined several priorities for both local governments and residents. The city says available alternative water sources should be used wherever legally possible, while irrigation efforts should focus first on young trees (up to five years old), followed by newly planted shrubs, flower beds and perennial plants.

Lawns, however, are no longer considered the highest priority. Officials noted that grass is generally capable of recovering after periods of drought, provided its root system survives. The immediate objective is therefore keeping lawns alive rather than keeping them green.

Mulch instead of more water

Another recommendation is to cover soil with grass clippings, wood chips, hay or other organic material. According to Dezsényi, mulch not only reduces evaporation but also protects soil from overheating, making it one of the simplest and most effective water-saving measures available.

Residents asked to help save young trees

FŐKERT is also appealing directly to Budapest residents to help water newly planted street trees. The city recommends giving each young tree 50 to 100 litres of water per watering session so that moisture reaches deep enough into the soil to have a lasting effect.

Residents are encouraged to use the Beeco mobile application, which maps thousands of young public trees across Budapest and several other Hungarian cities, making it easier for volunteers to find trees in need of watering.

Fountains switched off to save water

As part of the emergency response, FŐKERT has already shut down all 40 ornamental fountains and waterfalls under its management. Dezsényi said the same principle should apply elsewhere, urging people to minimise the use of swimming pools and other non-essential facilities that consume significant amounts of water and energy. An operational task force is expected to finalise Budapest’s broader climate emergency strategy in the coming days.
